speechtext: It is twenty minutes after eleven now, Mr. Speaker, and the motion calls for having the order for private bills taken up at eleven o'clock. Private members have an opportunity at eight o'clock this evening of taking up private bills for an hour, and I understand that as a result of conferences some of the difficulties that were anticipated have been removed. I think that we should allow the business of the House to proceed in the regular way and take up private bills at eight o'clock.

If we were perfectly sure that one hour would be sufficient to take care of the private bills on the order paper, or if we were perfectly sure that that hour would be extended to give ample time to take care of these private bills, I would be quite prepared to withdraw the motion, but we have no such assurance. We have had the experience in this chamber of the one hour allotted to private bills on Tuesday and Friday being wholly taken up with the discussion of one bill; in fact, we have had the experience this session not only of that one

hour in the evening being taken up but of all of Monday being used on some two or three occasions to discuss one bill. At the present time there are on the order paper many private bills, some of which are of great importance, and I fail to see the wisdom or the justice of so carrying on our legislative affairs as to block any legislation that any person or any corporation desires. Therefore, I feel like pressing this motion, Mr. Speaker, until we have some assurance that justice will be done by those who come here for legislation.
I ask under this motion that rule 25 in relation thereto be suspended. Rule 25 provides that private bills may be taken up on Monday, also on Tuesday and Friday evenings for one hour from eight until nine p.m. As the session advances, we are aill well aware that the government takes over Monday for government business, and that cuts us down to only two hours in the week for private bills. During the greater part of this session we have been cut down to the two hours time, because, as I purpose to show, practically all of the other time has been taken up in what we might call a futile discussion.
We are also told in our book of rules what the object of a private bill is. Under rule 88, paragraph 670 says:
The object of a private bill is to alter the law relating to some particular -locality or to confer rights on, or relieve from liability, some particular person or body of persons.
I think we are agreed in this chamber that the legislation in regard to any private bill is more or less useful. We have a great many divorce bills brought in under private legislation, bills respecting patents, bills respecting railway charters and bills respecting the organization of different companies. These matters are of great importance, and during this session, our time has been expended in such a way that these important matters of private legislation have not had due consideration in this chamber. We met here on Thursday, December 9, and on Wednesday, December 15, we adjourned after sitting for five days. I think during those five days we made a record for disposing expeditiously of matters before the House. We met again on Tuesday, February 8, and this is the 12th day of April, a matter of forty^seven sitting days since our adjournment. Counting to-day's sitting, we will have sat for fifty-two days during this present session of parliament.
I am not going to deal with what has been done on all the days but I would like to point out how the time allowed for private bills legislation has been expended. We had Bill No. 78, an act respecting the Montreal,
fMr. Oarmichad.]
Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company introduced on Friday, the 25th of February. After our adjournment we met on February 8, and on Friday, February 25, this very important bill was introduced. It was discussed on Friday, again discussed on March 1 for an hour, again on March 4 for one hour, and on Monday, March 7, it took practically -the entire day. On Tuesday, March 8, it was again discussed for one hour. On Friday, March 11, it was again discussed for an hour and on Monday, March 14, another day was spent on it. On Tuesday, March 15, and on Friday, March 18, another hour of each sitting was consumed. On Tuesday, March 15, and on Friday, March 18, another hour each day was devoted to it. On Monday, March 21, it was taken up again. On Tuesday,	March	22,	another	hour	wasoccupied. On Friday, March 25, and again on Monday,	March	28,	another	hour	wasconsumed with this bill. So that four Mondays and eight other days, an hour each day, were taken up with this measure-a total of twelve of	the	allotted	days	forprivate bills was consumed in the discussion of Bill No.	78. I	am	not going to	say
whose fault that was. I am simply pointing out what has actually happened, and the result has been that it has so held up other legislation as to leave us in the position we are now placed in, and it is possible that the other private measures cannot be taken care of before prorogation.
If, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggests we follow the regular procedure and take up private bills to-night from eight until nine o'clock, that will give us one hour for the consideration of private bills. But our rules are so framed that one bill may take the entire hour, and then if unanimous consent of the House is asked to continue beyond nine o'clock so as to take care of the other private bills, it is possible for one objector to block that procedure. We have had evidence of that recently in this chamber. If we propose to extend the time beyond nine o'clock one member can object and thus block consideration of private bills. I need not point out to hon. members that to-night is the last opportunity we will have for taking care of private bill legislation in this chamber, and if what has happened on past occasions should occur to-night, one bill, or possibly two bills, may consume the entire hour, and if someone who is not desirous of seeing certain legislation enacted should object to an extension beyond the hour, private bill legislation will be blocked. I claim that is not fair. No private legislation is introduced

Motion respecting Private Bills
in this House unless some person or persons are interested in it and desirous of having it enacted. I do not say that all private bills should be passed in this House, but all of them should be given fair consideration. If the majority of members favour any private legislation which is introduced in this House, such legislation should be enacted into law, but it certainly is most unfair and unjust for this House to have itself tied hand and foot by rules so that it is impossible for any private legislation to be given fair consideration and enacted into law. After the consideration of private bills in this House they require to go to the Senate. I am not just sure how speedily the upper chamber moves, but if they move no more speedily than we in this chamber do it will take some time to consider before prorogation all the private bills on the order paper. I am assuming that prorogation will take place in the near future. In fact, it was stated on Saturday by the Prime Minister that they were prepared to go on with any of the estimates. The leader of the government told the House on Saturday that they were practically through with their legislation and that we could be prepared to deal with the estimates. In that case we can look forward to prorogation in the very near future.
Since the disposal of Bill No. 78 we have had experience of another bill blocking private legislation, Bill No. 107, respecting the Sun Life Assurance Company. speechtext: Mr. G. R. GEARY (South Toronto) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 336, to amend the Railway Act, 1919 (investigation of subsidiary of telephone or telegraph companies).

subtopic: INVESTIGATION OF SUBSIDIARY OF TELEPHONE OR TELEGRAPH COMPANIES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION OF SUBSIDIARY OF TELEPHONE OR TELEGRAPH COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to extend the jurisdiction of the Dominion Board of Railway Commissioners. There are companies, one of which is in my mind, having to do with telephones and telegraphs, under the jurisdiction of the board. These companies may have their affairs investigated by the board with a view to ascertaining their profits, or what return it is fair to allow them by way of price they charge the consumer of their product.
Such oompany may have a great part of its business in the hands of a subsidiary company, which company-as in the case in my mind- is controlled by the company under the jurisdiction of the board and feeds on the parent company by virtue of having practically a monopoly in the sale of the products required by the parent company. That subsidiary company may, and in the case I have in mind does, make tremendous profits. With the parent company it does upwards of twelve or thirteen million dollars' worth Of business out of a total turnover of twenty million dollars. The purpose of the bill is to enable the Board of Railway Commissioners to ascertain whether profits made by the subsidiary company should be paid in the form of dividends to the parent company instead of their being put away into reserve or dealt with in such a way as to be concealed. If the profits were turned over to the parent company they would to that extent relieve the consumer of the product.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ALBERTA COAL CONDITION OF MINERS-TRANSPORTATION TO EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House goes into supply I regret the necessity which compels me t'o introduce a subject which I would wish had not arisen at this late date of the session. During the past few days I have received a series of telegrams describing a pitiable condition in the province from which I come, and particularly in the constituency which I represent. On the orders of the day the leader of the opposition read a telegram from the Lethbridge board of. trade relating to conditions there, and I now wish to place on Hansard one or two other telegrams which describe very vividly the conditions in my own constituency. On April 2, I received this telegram:
There are about two thousand mine workers out of work at present in the Drumheller valley. This has caused great distress and we would urge upon you the necessity for parliament taking immediate action to relieve the suffering of these men and their families which is growing more intense each passing week in any possible way you may determine.
I did my duty on that occasion and drew the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) to the condition indicated by this telegram. While the reply he gave me may have been the only one he could give, it was wholly unsatisfactory and unsympathetic. In effect he said that an investigation was being made by the Department of Labour into these conditions, but in the meantime the suffering is continuing. I now come to the second telegram, as follows:
Provincial government investigation-
Which was undertaken much more speedilj' than the investigation by this government:
-discloses acute distress in Drumheller. Hundreds of miners idle owing to shut down and no credit available. Immediate resumption of work in mines best solution. Your immediate cooperation and action earnestly solicited. Work only possible solution, reply early.
That telegram is signed by the secretary and president of Local 59 of the United Mine Workers' Association of America. I now come to the telegram which I received this morning, and to which I would call the attention of the Minister of Immigration, reminding him of the pleas made from this side of the House from time to time that some action be taken to protect the people against the utterly unjust, misleading, inaccurate and false promises made by shipping immigration agents and others to induce people to come to this country in the belief that they will be provided with steady employment at remunerative wages. This telegram which is dated April 11, is as follows:
Immigrants arriving Drumheller promised work coal mines quite number here now without funds and charge on community. Please advise government unless they can provide work through Ontario market to have immigrants directed elsewhere. Our own unemployment problem with mines closed too serious to countenance further immigration here.
That is signed by the Drumheller board of trade, whose members certainly are not of the radical type, and who would not put words of this kind into a telegram for presentation to this House if the situation did not compel them to do so. The next telegram is the one placed on record by the leader of the opposition this morning, and is as follows:
Resolution passed joint meeting subdistrict board miners union and coal committee board of trade Lethbridge. Whereas mines in this district practically shut down and other employment impossible for miners, resolved that we press federal government to take immediate steps relieve situation. Wider markets essential. We urge that railway commission cost report be brought in at once.
This House will recall that just over a year ago, on February 13, 1925, as a result of the efforts made by members of the House from t.he province from which I come, the administration were induced to bring in an order in council instructing the Board of Railway Commissioners to undertake an investigation into the actual cost of transporting coal for a special seasonal movement, which order in council urged the railway commission to undertake an immediate investigation. It was not the intention of the government nor indeed of those associated with the government to have the railway commission unduly delay this hearing. Then what happened? First of all, the basis of the inquiry was to be the out of pocket cost, that is, the cost exclusive of the expenses the railway would have to meet whether or not this coal was moved; the railway board were directed to report on the cost both exclusive and inclusive of that expense.
On February 24, 1926, Mr. Woods, counsel for the province of Alberta, speaking on this occasion for the province of Ontario as well.
2316	COMMONS
Alberta Coal-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
asked the board to set a date for a hearing at which would be determined what information the provinces would need from the railways in order to complete their case. On April 16, 1926, such a hearing took place and the railways were directed to provide counsel with a great quantity of information which was considered essential. It took all summer for the railways to amass this information; there certainly must have been a great deal of it, or else there must have been some very unnecessary delay. The experts came together, but by the fall the board were engaged on the general freight rate inquiry, so the investigation into the coal rates drifted along. An attempt was made by Mr. Woods on behalf of Alberta and Ontario in December last, because of the urgency of this question and because of the absolute need of having the board report to parliament before prorogation, to have the board take up this inquiry as the first order of business after they reconvened in January, 1927, and it was believed that the inquiry would not take more than two or three days. This the board definitely refused to do under a judgment given on December 16, 1926, in which they stated that they would not take up the coal rate inquiry which was of such immediate importance until the general freight rate inquiry was concluded. On February 10, 1927, Mr. Woods representing Alberta and Mr. Lawson representing Ontario again brought the matter before the railway board with the object of avoiding any delay in going on with the coal inquiry as soon as the general freight rate inquiry was over, and the railways then insisted that they would need two months after their experts were released from the general freight rate inquiry, to enable them to prepare their figures for the second inquiry. As it was then thought that the general freight rates inquiry would be finished by March 15, the board ordered a preliminary meeting of the experts of the two provinces and of the railway companies on May 15. two months after they were expected to conclude the general freight rate inquiry. At this meeting both sides were to produce their figures of costs and the points of difference would be defined. The final hearing on these points was to take place on June 7, 1927.
An attempt was also made in this House by hon. members in the U.F.A. group to induce the Minister of Railways or the administration as a whole to take such steps they might properly take to get the railway board to expedite this hearing. The order in council which I have under my hand was particularly specific. It asked for an immediate examina-

tion and report upon the actual out of pocket cost of moving the coal. Why was it utterly necessary that this be immediate? Because we all understood that it would take some time to gather the facts and for the board to make and present its findings. That being the case, we realized that if action was to be taken at the coming session of parliament, the findings of the board should be in the hands of the government during the session and preferably early in the session. Every effort was made by this group and by our Alberta counsel before the board to have this action taken that was so necessary. The chairman of the board was advised again and again that if he delayed this hearing, the solution of the question as regards Alberta would go over for another season and it would not be dealt with until the next session of this parliament, with the result that no coal would move to Ontario for another year.
As a result of the decisions laid down by the board, we have now exactly the situation which we feared. We have a situation in which the board's refusal to make this inquiry in January last has now so delayed the question that the inquiry will not take place until after this House has prorogued and so too late for action by this parliament. That action by this parliament will be necessary is quite apparent from the wording of the order in council which does not give to the board any power to set the rate. All the board has power to do is to determine the cost rate on the values agreed upon between the railways and representatives of the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Once the board has found that and reported thereon to the government or parliament, its duties have ceased. It is then for the government to bring in statutory legislation making that rate effective.
As hon. gentlemen can readily see, the desperate conditions in ithe province in which I represent one constituency would certainly indicate that some remedial measure should be taken. I have simply this to suggest and I took the liberty of suggesting it the other day to the minister and following it up by letter. Having consulted with him previously in the matter, with his permission I will read a letter which I wrote him in that connection: Ottawa, Ontario, April 7, 1927. Hon. Charles Stewart,
Minister of the Interior,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Stewart,
Following up my conversation with you of yesterday, in which I brought to your attention the necessity for some action by parliament at this session to enable the government to bring into effect whatever cost rate may be deter-

Alberta Coal-Mr. JellifJ
mined by the Board of Railway Commissioners as a result of the investigation into the actual cost of the transportation of coal.
May I recall to your attention the nature of our conversation-you will recollect that an order in council instructed the board to make this investigation and no powers were given to your board to set the rate that might be determined to be used as the coal rate. It is therefore quite clear to me that should the board of its own volition, attempt to set this rate (which of course is most improbable) the railways would at once serve an injunction upon that body.
I expressed the opinion to you if the Alberta coal operators are ever to secure a portion of the Ontario market, it will be necessary for the administrators to introduce a bill providing for a special seasonal cost rate for the movement of the coal.
I do most earnestly urge upon you, as the minister representing the province from which we both come, the necessity to secure from this parliament before it prorogues the necessary powers to enable you to put into effect the rate that will be allowed by the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Yours very truly,
This is signed by myself. I have already briefly reviewed my reasons for doing this. Some exception may be taken by hon. gentlemen that to give such a blanket authority to a minister would be a dangerous matter. I submit that it would not in this case for this reason. If the out-of-pocket cost rate to be found by the board is to be at all effective in the movement of coal, that rate will have to be no more than $7 a ton. From my examination of this question, from the evidence given before our coal committees year after year by experts of both railways, I am satisfied that the out-of-pocket cost rate will vary somewhere between $6 and $7. I am satisfied therefore that the only spread, the only blanket right that need be granted in this matter is to set a limitation within a matter of a few cents. I would be quite satisfied if the administration could now take authority to put into effect the cost rate when it is determined, if that cost rate is less than $7 and not more than $6. That leaves them within a limitation of $1 for this coal rate.
May I repeat that the condition in my province justifies drastic action by this House? The miners there-and I know them only too well-have from year to year periodic, seasonal employment scattered over a period of from three to four months during only two of which they will have constant labour, and during the balance of the year they are picking up jobs wherever they can. No int'ellli-gent effort is being made by provincial or federal labour bureaux to transport these men at reasonable railway rates so that they may find employment during the slack season in some other occupation and to bring them back to
the coal mines during the winter. Surely we ought to be able to work out some scheme whereby some occupations which are distinctly seasonal might be combined in order to spread employment over the whole year. There is a possibility in that direction; but in the meantime the crying need is market's for our coal.
We have ample coal of the finest quality for domestic purposes and there is no question as to the favour with which public opinion in Ontario has received our coal. The whole matter now rests with the administration. The people in this great province of Ontario will take the coal if they can get it at a reasonable rate. They are willing to pay within a reasonable margin of anthracite prices for it, and in passing I may say they are well advised in so being willing because, taking all in all, the wise householder can get as much heat value and with much less waste out of our Alberta coal than out of anthracite. However, at this stage of the session I do not want to go into the relative merits of our coal; it is indeed already well and favourably known.
I wish to ask now that the administration state definitely to me and to the House what their policy is going to be in this regard. I have not asked too much; all I have asked is that the cost rate to be determined by the board shall, as soon as determined and reported upon, be enacted into an effective measure so that the movement of coal may at once take place. The coal could start moving during the summer months when the rate would be in operation. The people of Ontario will welcome it with open arms, and they are accustomed to get in their coal supply during the summer months. Give them an opportunity to do that and you will enormously increase the prosperity and comfort of two of the great provinces of this Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I have the same telegram from the Lethbridge board of trade as that read by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) and referred to by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I am deeply sympathetic with this message. The situation there is such that we have to find a remedy for it. It exists and comes forward to trouble our councils year after year, and it is time, Mr. Speaker, that some definite steps be taken to meet this problem. True it is that the winter is over and the prairie demand for coal has diminished, and the men who are engaged in the mines may expect less employment than they have had during the cold winter season. It is also true that more or
2318	COMMONS
Alberta Coal-Mr. Heenan-Mr. Forke
less employment can be secured in the seeding operations which will soon be in full blast throughout the district which I represent, but at the same time that does not permanently and efficiently solve the problem which exists there. We have been chasing this problem from one side to the other during the last five years in which I have been a member of this House, and still we seem to be little closer to a solution of'it than we were five years ago. We have tried through orders in council, through references to the board of railway commissioners, and through the taking of evidence month after month and year after year to arrive at some basis for a settlement of'this problem, but as I said we are no closer to a solution than we were several years ago. I have got to the point myself where I feel that this problem can only be met definitely and finally by the passing of an act by this parliament fixing a rate at which coal from Alberta can be carried to the central provinces. That would put the question beyond all peradveniture of dispute. After such an act is passed, we can determine from actual experience how it works out, and if it fails to work ofut well, if we find that it places too big a burden on this country or upon the transportation system, it will be an easy matter for us to repeal that act. I want to point out to the Prime Minister that we have a precedent, and a very good precedent, for dealing with this matter in the way I suggest in the action we have taken in regard to freight rates in the maritime provinces, and the rates on grain and flour under the Crowsnest pass agreement.
I urge upon the government to bring forward a measure fixing a rate more or less based upon the investigations which have been carried on into the shipment of coal in trainload lots during the last four years. Let us try this method out and see if it works, so that we can definitely settle this problem for the good of our great coal mining industry.

speechtext:
In reply to the reference made to
the Minister of Labour by my good friend opposite, I may say that I received on April the first the same telegram that he did, and the very next day I had a man on the job looking into the situation, because I was not sure whether it was employment or unemployment relief that these men were asking for. The investigator is a very able man. He went into the coal district and there ascertained that the men were looking for work, not relief. I conveyed to the rest of my colleagues my suggestions as to the best ways and means of securing work for them, and that matter is still under consideration fMr. Jelliff.]	.	'
at the present time. I also took the matter up personally with Mr. Brownlee, the provincial premier, and he too is looking into the matter, all with the object of trying to provide work for the men in that district. I pointed out to Mr. Brownlee, when he was here, that if it was not a very serious affair and any financial assistance was required, I thought they ought to provide it locally, and he went back the same night for the purpose of going into the matter and conferring with me again.
The hon. member said that I did not give a very sympathetic answer. Well, the only thing I could do was to ascertain just what the real trouble was, and that message was the first intimation I had that there was any real trouble in the coal fields, and the very next day after receiving it I had a man investigating the situation right on the ground. He went right amongst the miners to find out what they wanted, and from all the correspondence it appears that they do not want relief, but work. That matter, as I say, is under consideration and I can assure my hon. friend that as far as I am concerned I shall do the very best I can.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
maintopic: SUPPLY-ALBERTA COAL CONDITION OF MINERS-TRANSPORTATION TO EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I might say a few words in reply to the hon. member's references to immigrants coming into this country. If we do not want immigrants, of course there is no more to be said. The trouble in Alberta in, the coal mines may be serious enough in itself, but after all, it is confined to the locality, and is a matter all by itself. There is no doubt that quite a number of immigrants are coming in, but the season has been very backward in western Canada and seeding has been delayed, and consequently there may be some little trouble for a time. Although I know and thoroughly believe that we need more population in this country, I am very well aware of the fact that you cannot have from 150,000 to 200,000 immigrants coming into a country in any one year without dislocating employment conditions to a certain extent. That is inevitable, but I have no hesitation in saying that six weeks from now no one will be idle in western Canada who is seeking employment.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): With regard to the problem brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), one would gather from his remarks that he believes that 'action by the railway commission, or by the government consequent upon extraordinary powers being

Alberta Coal-Mr. Dunning
given, to it by this parliament, might conceivably solve the present unemployment difficulty among the miners in Drumheller. I feel that he did not mean to convey that impression, but by linking the two things together he was apparently proposing a remedy for the presently existing disease.
I feel that he did not wish to convey that impression, but that was the impression I gathered from his remarks. On that point might I say this: I have very great doubts if any action by the railway commission or any action that is taken with respect to freight rates will eliminate the seasonal nature of work in the Alberta coal fields. Personally, having conducted somewhat of an examination into possible markets, I cannot see how it is possible to overcome completely the seasonal rush and the seasonal slack time in the Alberta coal fields with the markets at present in sight and in view of the time and manner in which the people in those markets wiH consent to take the coal made available to them by the mine operators of Alberta and other places.
But the problem goes very much deeper even than that. There is nothing to prevent the mines of Alberta from constantly enlarging their seasonal capacity. That factor, as my hon. friend well knows, is very largely the controlling one in mining operations. If there is a large seasonal demand, every mine will so equip itself with mechanical devices and labour to attempt to take the fullest possible advantage of that seasonal demand. When that is the case, inevitably there follows a slack time. I am not endeavouring to convey the impression that the problem is not possible of solution, but rather that it is not one that can be solved by devising some measure of freight rate relief as between Alberta and Ontario, although that, of course might be a mitigating factor. My hon. friend referred to the order in council of last February. I have it before me, and I think he will agree that -it does provide for the kind of examination into this matter which was desired by those most nearly interested, both in the coal producing sections of Alberta and in the coal consuming sections of Ontario.
I regret the delay on the part of the railway commission as much as he can possibly do. I might respectfully point out however that the work of the general rate inquiry has been very heavy. I am not now defending the railway commission, but I must remind the House that they are not supermen. There is only a certain amount of time in every day, and when counsel for the two provinces interested are also engaged in arguing the
matter of the general freight equalization, it is difficult to see how the railway commission could have moved much faster in connection with the coal rate inquiry. Everything the government could do to expedite the work of the commission with regard to this particular matter has, 'I assure my hon. friend, been done. I, personally, have made representations to the chairman in regard to the necessity for expedition. I now understand from what my hon. friend says-and it is confirmed in other ways-that a definite move is to be made, I think he said on May i5.

Perhaps I misunderstood my hon. friend in that regard. That was
certainly the impression I gathered! from his remarks, based as they were on telegrams calling attention to presently existing conditions. There is a very vital matter of principle involved, may I say, in any decision which may be reached by this parliament on this matter of freight rates on coal from Alberta to Ontario. We might adopt any one of several courses in relation thereto. For instance, should parliament say that the railway companies must haul coal without a cent of profit and let it go at that, or should parliament adopt the principle that the railway companies should charge a certain rate, and that part of the rate should be 'borne by the Dominion and part by the shippers of the coal? There are several ways of looking at the problem, and if I remember correctly, when it was my duty to introduce here not very long ago a measure having to do with the maritime provinces and their freight rates, the only opposition to it came from my hon. friends in that corner of the House, who are advocating in this connection the same general principle in respect of their coal industry with relation to the market of Ontario.

Mr. DUN Nils G:	My hon. friend draws a
fine distinction. Apparently he is willing, in

He draws a distinction between that and the measure adopted with respect to the maritime province freight rates of paying for the twenty per cent cut ordered by parliament. He is capable of drawing distinctions too fine for my understanding, because I can see very little difference between those two propositions in principle. However, that may be, the intention of the government with regard to the m'attter is well set out in the order in council, and I can say to my hon. friend, and others who may be interested, that the moment we get this information from the Board of Railway Commissioners as a government we will move in one of two directions. First, we intend to find out immediately from the nature of the re>-port received whether the railway commission would have authority to do anything to meet any of the recommendations made which might appear to have the effect desired. That would be one course. The second course would be that I might undertake, as Minister of Railways, immediately to confer with the management of the Canadian National Railways, at all events, and probably with the Canadian Pacific Railway, who, I presume, would also be willing to confer on the matter, as to how far the railways would be prepared to go in advance of the meeting of parliament, having regard to the information made available to the government as a result of the inquiry by the Board of Railway Commissioners. That is as far as the government is prepared to go at the moment, all with the objective of bringing if possible, some relief to the situation prior to the next meeting of parliament; but I do think this parliament will desire to express itself upon the principle involved in legislation which will create for the first time a special rate in respect of transportation of one commodity from one part of Canada to another part of Canada. A very wide and important principle is involved in that. But in so far as the government can move upon the basis of the information we expect to receive from the Board of Railway Commissioners, the government will move along lines designed to mitigate the situation and widen the market for Alberta coal.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have just a word to say in regard to this matter which has been introduced by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland). The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has stated that in this question there are certain principles at stake, and he has discussed them. But one great principle he has not discussed. The situation to-day is this; the miners of Alberta want work, and the people of Ontario want coal. The principle at stake is: shall the Canadian people use Canadian coal? That is the principle which this government should undertake to apply. It should have a definite policy to lay before the House. For the last six years this has been a perennial subject of debate; but we have got nowhere-we have reached no conclusion, we have relieved no situation. Now, to anyone who takes an interest in this question-and my direct interest is only that of an Ontario consumer-it is discouraging when one recalls how the treatment of this subject has been delayed. On that order in council passed in February, 1926, we have as yet had no action. The matter was referred to the Board of Railway Commissioners; there if rests. An intimation is given to the House to-day that probably in June some finding will be made by the Board of Railway Commissioners, or that they will begin to deal with the question.
That brings me to the constitution of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Justice is not being done in this country to-day in regard to railway rates, and has not been done for the last two or three years, the reason being that the Board of Railway Commissioners, as at present constituted, are unable to do the work which has been delegated fo them by the Railway Act and, in many instances, directed by this parliament. What are we going to do with that situation? It cannot go on as it is now. Is the government prepared to increase the personnel of that board and to divide it up, or is it prepared to divide up the present board, and allow us to have two boards sitting at the same time? If it requires the full membership of the present board to decide the cases which are referred to it, then it is quite within the range of possibility that there will be no finding on this coal question for another year, perhaps two years. What are the miners of Alberta and the people of Ontario to do in the meantime? There is a solution of this question, and so far as Ontario is concerned we complain of the delay in finding the solution.

But we have them in mind, and we expect action to be taken on all these questions, but I maintain that the fair thing to do is to let our position be made plain, that we are willing to allow the government a reasonable time to implement their promises. We expect them to take action on all these matters, but in the meantime I propose to adopt what I believe is the proper attitude towards the government, and give them a reasonable opportunity of satisfying maritime claims.

I want to say that I cannot at this time associate myself with the protest which has been uttered by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley), nor will I associate myself with protests made by any other member on this side of the House at this time in connection with the government's attitude on maritime claims. I realize that all the recommendations of the Duncan report have not been implemented by the government at this session, but my attitude is that as the Prime Minister has not closed the door with respect to the matters not dealt with, I am willing to give the government a fair chance to implement the complete Duncan report later, and I believe that most people of the maritimes are of this opinion.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Agriculture-live stock, including grants to exhibitions, feeder shows, etc., $1,280,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
As some hon. members would
like to leave before this evening, I think I will take the three major votes first, Nos. 44, 45 and possibly 46. The item No. 44 has been under discussion intermittently all session, and I presume something will be said with regard

to it. This vote includes grants for exhibitions, which account for nearly $300,000, leaving a little less than $1,000,000 for live stock.
What exhibitions are benefitting by this grant?

This vote covers
both summer and winter 'fairs throughout Canada. A certain number of summer fairs are allocated to each province. Starting on the Pacific, the four western provinces have two summer fairs allotted to them, for which they receive $5,000 each. The two older provinces, Ontario and Quebec, have three summer fairs allotted to them and they receive the same amount. The three maritime provinces are each allotted one fair, and they receive the same grant. I think that lonstituites about seventeen of what we call 'A" fairs, all capable of drawing as high as $5,000 each. Then there are about twenty-one "B" fairs, a grade lower than the others. They are not allocated according to provinces and seem to have no particular plans in connection with their establishment-no particular getting-on place or no particular getting-off place. These get a flat rate of $1,500 each. In addition to that there are about eleven or twelve winter fairs extending from Amherst on the east to Vancouver on the west, including Ottawa, Toronto, Chatham and London, in Ontario, and Valleyfield, Three Rivers and Ste. Scholastique in Quebec, Amherst representing the three maritime provinces. In the four western provinces, Manitoba has one, Saskatchewan and Alberta have two each, and British Columbia one.
Would the minister give us his opinion as to how a grant to one of these big fairs is any encouragement to the live stock industry?
Does my hon. friend mean the larger fairs, the "A" fairs, Toronto or Ottawa, or any of them?
I am referring to class " A " fairs. Is the grant made direct to the society?

Direct to the association. It is generally understood that where live stock growers assemble their products in competition with each other it always stimulates a desire for better and greater production, and it is a means of advertising, without which the stock men usually would be out of luck. As a matter of fact it usually costs the stock man about as much to pay his way to the fair as the prizes amount to. Then they have the advertising, which means that there is a balance coming to them. The

Supply-Agriculture
people get to know about their class of stock, and a friendly competition is usually such a stimulant that it develops stock raising to a great extent. This applies to all the exhibitions whether large or small. The most primitive or youngest exhibition in a little village of two or three hundred inhabitants, representing a large rural district, will perform in a small measure the same object for the people locally. But it is not so notieable because they are not quite in the same class as the breeders of pure bred live stock.
Why do you not spend the grant by giving prizes for live stock?

The major portion of these grants, in fact all of them, were given on the basis of the live stock exhibit. That is specified. My hon. friend knows that it was a perambulating exhibition from one province to another. It never went to Prince Edward Island, but they got a special grant instead. Just before the war this perambulating Dominion fair was held at Victoria. Subsequently it was divided into interpro-vinoial fairs, these developed into "A" and "B" fairs, and these again into winter fairs. I have been endeavouring for some time to find a getting-off place so as to withdraw from this expenditure.

Mr. Chairman, I had an opportunity of speaking to the minister not long ago on the subject of cooperative marketing, and I was pleased to find that he shared my enthusiasm. I call cooperative marketing the business end of farming. I believe if we had to choose between this form of marketing and fairs we would favour the former as conferring the greater advantage on farmers. In the Department of Agriculture, and perhaps in the Department of Trade and Commerce, there should be officials who are specialists in this subject, for it is no easy matter for a number of farmers to take up cooperative marketing. The average farmer may not know exactly what to produce, and what he does produce he sometimes finds difficulty in disposing of at remunerative prices. This is where the cooperative marketing specialist will be useful. I hope the minister will take steps along the lines I have suggested. I believe that if such an official explained to farmers in different parts of the country the practical advantages of up-to-date cooperative marketing it would add very materially to their welfare.

Mr. Chairman,
cooperative marketing has taken a decided grip not only of the people of Canada but of
the whole continent. I think nothing gave such a stimulus to cooperative marketing as the difficulties which faced our farmers after the war. Twenty years ago it became an objective on the prairies, where we were having very hard times, and we adopted it as a measure of necessity. The great wheat pools on the prairies are farmers' organizations, and to-day they are conducted without any governmental aid. This applies also to Ontario. But it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the time is ripe for the federal authority to become active. I have taken the ground recently that we might very well drop off some of our provincial activities and turn our attention to cooperative marketing. As a matter of fact, while we have not a distinct branch devoted to this work, we have been engaged in these activities for some time and have encouraged the cooperative marketing of poultry, eggs, sheep and swine. As soon as I knew the nature of the Duncan fruit report of two years ago I took the responsibility of calling the fruit men from all over the Dominion to a conference in this city. We paid their expenses and discussed with them the best methods of national salesmanship in view of the selling methods that the Duncan report had condemned. If my hon. friend has a first-class man available for this work of cooperative marketing I am in the field for one if I can get him past the Civil Service Commission.
Are you referring to me?

Yes. There is another limitation. I have branches of my department in about eighteen buildings scattered throughout the city and across in Hull as well as on the experimental farm, and I rather dread the thought of establishing one more branch in one more building. We have this year in the estimates half a million dollars for a departmental building. The hon. member for St. John-Albert and all others who believe in cooperative marketing will facilitate the establishment of a branch devoted to the subject if they will help me secure a wing of this prospective building so I may have my staff within immediate call to confer on any particular question. Until that time arrives I hesitate to appoint any more branch heads.

I suggest to the minister that he might hasten the time when he will have completed the new office of the Department of Agriculture. By eliminating grants to class " A " fairs he would have a good deal of money to secure the building he needs and he would use the rest of the grant to maintain a bureau of cooperative marketing. Such a
Supply-Agriculture

bureau was established in the United States two years ago and I remember seeing in the Congressional Record the statement that they had appropriated $200,000 per annum as a start. The minister might very well reduce the vote of $200,000 to these big fairs, or cut it out and use the money for the creation of a bureau of cooperative marketing. It may be that the grant to these fairs does some good, but I believe the fairs would run just the same whether they got the grant or not. The minister since coming into office has adopted the policy of cutting down the grants particularly to the small fairs, and if the small fairs can get along without this assistance the larger ones surely ought to be able to do so. The larger fairs are held in places where there is a large population. The gate receipts are good and the fairs can carry on without a grant. I labour this point now because I think it would be of much more assistance to the live stock industry if the minister were to establish a bureau of cooperative marketing such as I suggest, than continuing grants to fairs. I want to compliment the minister for the sympathy he has shown towards cooperative marketing, as evidenced in the live stock bill brought down the other day. He tried to meet the wishes of the cooperators in that regard and I wish to thank him for what he has done. I hope however he will go further and set up a bureau of cooperative marketing and, instead of asking for more money from parliament, take from the grants to the class " A " fairs whatever he needs for the purpose. The minister might tell us what is done with the million dollars that are voted for live stock. The farmers are anxious to know to what use the money is put. The minister proposes to cut off the money he has been spending in furnishing pure bred sires to cattlemen. He has been cutting down the grants to the smaller fairs and still he is asking for the same amount he has been voted before. What use is made of the grant under live stock?
I have been trying to eliminate the votes to fairs and I hope to have in my hon. friend a champion in this regard.
You will so far as the class " A " fairs are concerned, anyway.

The live stock vote is divided as follows: For the horse division there is $149,000. My hon. friend is familiar with the horse club policy inaugurated in 1913 or 1914 throughout Canada. That policy, I think, has done a lot of good. I do not know how long it will be continued but I

may observe that there has been no agitation for its abolition. To the cattle division there is devoted $260,000. There has been some discussion in the House off and on with regard to some alteration in policy in that direction, but the vote has not been reduced inasmuch as we have 1,400 bulls throughout Canada at the present time, and the cost of upkeep is considerable. The cost of service therefore, during the next couple of years, will be practically what it has been all along. For sheep and swine we are asking $230,000, and very much the same form of assistance is given in this regard. It has been a question with me-and I frankly admit it-how far we should go in promoting poultry, sheep and swine production in the various provinces. I have had a strenuous time, as my hon. friend realizes, endeavouring to get the provinces to take over some of the work in this field, but there is still a good deal left to be done in the maritime provinces. We have felt rather sympathetic towards them. No one loved them, and I wanted to let them know that at any rate the Department of Agriculture did. But we have been engaging in activities that are decidedly provincial and I think we shall continue for some time yet to do so. When we have had so much difficulty in weaning the rest of Canada from some of these services hon. gentlemen will realize what a whale of a time we shall have in the maritime provinces. I do not want to make life miserable for myself by eliminating too many of these activities all at once. It is all good work and whoever initiated it deserves our commendation. For the administration of the various stockyards, of which there are eight or ten in Canada, we are spending $50,000, and for exhibitions and judges the amount allotted is $200,000. The latter is exclusive of the winter fair at Toronto, which receives $35,000 per annum. We do not set up exhibits in regular places, but at the semi-provincial fairs and the smaller fairs throughout the country we do so whenever requested. They are anxious in some of these places to have the experimental farm set up an exhibit because it helps to advertise the products of Canada while at the same time it makes for the success of the exhibition. The national live stock movement, as the committee understands, embraces a vast number of live stock associations. The organization comprises live stock institutes from horses down to foxes, with pedigrees that are recorded in the National Live Stock Association. Mr. Brant has charge of this section.

Supply-Agriculture

How nearly do the fees
in connection with live stock pay for the work?
This is a straight grant. The officer referred to is not in the department. The money helps the association to carry on its work.
What is the amount of the grant?

With regard to the cost
of the administration of stock yards, the $50,000 is rather high, is it not?

There are several
yards-two in Saskatchewan, two in Alberta, one in Manitoba, one in Toronto and one in Montreal. We have to keep a staff of at least three, and of course the cost in connection therewith comes out of the amount. For printing and stationery the amount asked is $43,000; general, $15,000; and advertising $25,000. We have not done very much in the matter of advertising for the reason that the vote would not permit anything extensive. The total of the amounts thus expended is $1,280,000.

The minister said his
department loved the maritime provinces. How is it that while agriculture is recognized to be the best industry in that part of Canada the Duncan report contains no recommendation in its behalf?
I fancy Sir Andrew Duncan thought I was doing all that was good for them at the present time.

Does the grading of live
stock come under this vote?
Yes.

How much is used for
grading?

There is only one
class of live stock in the world graded on the hoof, and that is hogs. Sheep and swine together take up $230,000, and for grading purposes we have a staff of twenty-two, established three years ago. I will give, later on, information in that regard.

Is there any change in
the grading system?

There wa3 very
nearly a pronounced change about a month ago, but I took the responsibility for calling a conference of those who constituted the original gathering in the fall of 1921 which 32649-148
met to formulate a policy in connection with the building up of a better bacon trade in Canada based on a sound bacon hog. That conference was held in 1921 and at it there were representatives of the departments of agriculture of the nine provinces. I do not know whether all the departments were represented, but at any rate they were invited. Invitations were extended also to the railway companies, the swine breeders' associations and the live stock unions. Since that time two or three organizations have come into existence, and they of course will add to the representation at the forthcoming conference. The conference is to be held towards the close of next week to ascertain the next step to be taken in the matter of developing the bacon trade of Canada in the light of present conditions.

It is to be held in
Ottawa?

Yes, the packers
have taken the ground that they cannot afford to pay the 10 per cent premium. They have been losing money, they claim, on that account and also because of changed conditions in Europe, but I persuaded them not to depart from the undertaking of 1921, at least until all those who had entered into that arrangement had had an opportunity of talking the matter over.

What advertising is being
done now?

In the year just
passed we spent about $10,000 in advertising in the farm papers, and occasionally in others. We have done some advertising also in the old country papers.

I do not agree with my
hon. friend (Mr. Coote) in his proposal to wipe out the grants ,to fairs. I have been brought up, I might almost say, in the live stock industry in Canada, and having observed the development of these exhibitions I know what work they have done towards the improvement of our cattle business. I do not think we have yet reached the point where we can afford seriously to cramp the work of these exhibitions. At the same time I fully realize the importance of assisting cooperative marketing wherever we possibly can, because I am a firm believer in the fact that the farmer is certainly entitled to whatever he earns, whether through live stock or the cultivation of the soil. I want to see the farmer assisted in every possible way, not only through cooperative marketing but through every other means that will bring to
