Supply-Agriculture
him the greatest return for what he is doing. I would like to see the cost of shipping his exportable products to tide-water reduced to the lowest possible figure as well.
Now I propose to take up a few minutes of the time of the House in looking over the cattle situation as it is to-day and as it affects the live stock producer of Canada. We in Canada have three markets, the British market, the United States market and our home market; we export about 15 per cent of all the beef cattle produced in this country, which means that we must consume about * 85 per cent of our production at home. The British market has been a great help to us, since it has created a competitive market for our products and has a stiffening effect upon our prices at home. This market was good from the removal of the embargo until 1926, increasing each year until that period, when it fell off to some extent. Our exports to the British market in 1925 were 110,000 head, but in 1926 this number was reduced to some 70,000, which is explained by several causes. First there was a severe coal strike, which reduced their consuming power; foot and mouth disease was also rife in the country, making it dangerous to handle cattle. There was a depression of business as a result of the strike and also a meat war in the Argentine between British and American packing interests, with the result that a vast amount of cheap Argentine beef was thrown on the market. This all had its effect on the British market and accounted for the falling off in our exports during 1926. However, I think prospects are better for the future, remembering that the freight rate has now been reduced to $15 per head, and that in addition there is a general improvement in the mother country. I had the pleasure the other day of meeting a gentleman just returned from the old country, a man in business on the Pacific coast, and I was very glad to hear from him that a feeling of optimism was being developed in England that the Britishers are gradually regaining those markets which they lost some time ago, and that they expect better business in the near future. This should assist to a great extent in providing a better market for our Canadian beef producers.
The market in the United States, of course, is one with which wTe would naturally fall in line if it were not for the barrier raised against us. In 1920 I think we reached the peak of our exportation to the United States, when we shipped something like 520,000 head of cattle. The emergency tariff came into effect m 1921, followed by the Fordney tariff
fMr. Tolmie.]
of 1926, with the result that our shipments to the United States have been very much reduced. Last year we exported to that country only 90,000 head of cattle, and the year before we exported about 85,000 head.

I think the figure is
290,000 head.

Exported to the United
States last year?
Yes, for the year ending March 31, 1926.

No. In 1925 we exported
to the United States 86,748 head, and in 1926. 90,000; those are the figures I have. That United States market takes about 65 per cent of our feeder cattle, that is, cattle which are taken to the corn belt and fattened up foi the market at a later time of the year, and I think we can be proud of the fact that on the ranges of western Canada we produce a very high type of feeder, perhaps as good as can be produced in the world. The market in the United States would be very suitable to us on account of its close proximity, but because of the tariff we are not able to take advantage of it to the extent we would wish.
Perhaps a brief glance at the cattle situation in the United States may be of interest. The cattle population of the United States before the war was about 58,000,000 head, in 1921 this had risen to 67,184,000 head, and in 1922 to 67,264,000, while in 1926 the figure receded again to about 58,000,000. In 1914 the human population of the United States was 97,927 516; in 1925 that had risen to 115,378,094, oi an increase of 9 per cent in eleven years. The beef consumption per capita in the United States is 61.1 pounds, and in Canada 74.9 pounds. The marketing of cattle in the United States has not shown any increase from 1919 to 1925; in fact there has been something of a falling off. In 1919 the cattle marketed amounted to 24,623,000, while in 1925 that figure had fallen to 24,067,000. About 40 per cent of that includes dairy cattle, stockers, feeders, and calves, and so we must deduct that from the other leaving about 14,978,920 head of cattle in the United States for slaughter purposes. Those cattle average about 506.16 pounds per carcass, so that the total beef production of the United States is about 7,581,730,147 pounds. The yearly consumption amounts to 7,049,601,543 pounds, so that there is a surplus of 532,128,604 pounds that must find a market somewhere oustide of the United States, or enough to support S,-723,255 of an increased population in that country. The average annual increase in popu-

Supply-Agriculture
lation is 1,586,416, so that unless the United States is able to secure new sources of supply of cattle, the gradual increase in population should get rid of that surplus in a period of about six years, and then the United States would cease to be an exporting country in regard to beef cattle. I do not say it is impossible for them to increase their production of beef, but no doubt that beef will be produced at a higher cost, because in the United States the ranching country where cheap beef is produced was about gone some time ago.
I do not think the 90,000 head of cattle that we sent to the United States last year seriously interferes with the market in that country because it is so small in proportion to the large volume of beef that is handled. As an indication that this might be true, let me say that the secretary of agriculture in his report of 1925 refers to the splendid, beneficial effects of the tariff as affecting dairy produce, fruit, wheat, sheep, flax, sugar beet and sugar cane, but he makes no reference whatever to its advantage in connection with the beef industry.
We come now to our home market, the most important one of all as I pointed out a while ago, using about 85 per cent of our products. In 1926 about a million head of cattle went through our live stock yards. Probably half a million more are slaughtered in country places, on farms and so forth. We find however that a tremendous raft of scrubs go through our live stock yards; more than 50 per cent of the animals passing through our yards are graded as common and look as though they were raised in some cases for speed and trained a little fine at that. There is a difference of about $30 a head between grades good and common, showing what a tremendous loss our farmers are suffering as a result of, first, losing in the weight of the animal and, second, on account of its poor quality having the price lowered again. Less than six per cent of our cattle as they pass through our yards are of sufficiently good quality to compete with the 2,000,000 Argentine cattle that are exported every year. Only about 10 or 15 per cent of our cattle going through our yards are of sufficiently high quality to obtain the highest average price. Therefore this is a clean-cut indication that 85 per cent of our cattle are badly in need of improvement not only in breeding but in more liberal feeding.

How do our cattle compare in Great Britain with cattle from the Argentine?
32649-I4SJ

As regards the quality of
Argentine cattle, I never before saw such uniform beef as I saw in the Smithfield market from the Argentine. The beef that the British market has taken from the Argentine is on the average considerably ahead of ours.
What do we find in regard to our beef as it goes on the market? Consumers in Canada have very little knowledge regarding the quality of meat. We eat more beef than we do of all other meats in Canada and we would eat a great deal more if we were only sure of the quality. We find that in Canada we buy tender steaks instead of tasty steaks. That is why we find on many of our tables what I call a two-way steak, probably secured from an animal that is poor, a steak that is taken from a tenderloin. I call it a twoway steak because in addition to being tender it is also tasteless. The cheaper cuts are usually bought by the working people, and in this regard again no knowledge is shown of the improved quality between beef from the finished animal and beef from one of the poorer kind. We find too that much of our beef going on the market is tough and unpalatable, and after living around our boarding houses in this country for a number of years since I entered politics about ten years ago, I have come to the conclusion that we in Canada are a tough, strong-jawed people. What does this cheap trash do? It takes up the goodly part of the market that would be supplied by the better quality. The man who buys, let us say, a roast for his Sunday dinner, finds that roast is of poor quality, and the result is that he simply gives up the eating of beef for a week or ten days and buys mutton or pork or chicken. Herbivorous people became numerous during the war and immediately after; a campaign was started to encourage the eating of more salads and fruits, and this was carried to such an extent that it reduced the consumption of beef by some millions of pounds on this continent. In fact some of these people pushed the matter so far that they became almost wholly herbivorous and would have become cud-chewers in another generation or two. This might have reached the stage where they would have simply turned their families out on the lawn in the summertime and they would rustle for themselves.
What are we going to do to meet the situation? I was much interested in the Live Stock Act which was brought up the other day for amendment in which there was a proposal for beef grading. This would be of great advantage; but we must carry on a campaign of education and teach our consumers to buy the better cuts, so that w*
Supply-Agriculture

may in that way bring back the higher prices to the man who takes the trouble and goes to the expense of producing an animal of high quality. The great difficulty is this, that while the United States. Canada and some other countries are much interested in beef grading, they have not yet evolved a plan that will protect the consumer. Under ordinary conditions a man might buy a second class or No. 2 cow, cut her up into steaks, and I would defy anybody buying those steaks, in many cases to tell the difference between them and a steak from a No. 1 steer. The result is that there must be some means of educating the people and of clearly designating the difference between No. 1 and No. 2 beef.
That is the problem which is being faced in the United States now where they have several committees created which are being backed up with a good deal of money. These committees are carrying on a careful investigation, and in a year or two we shall be in a good position to benefit from what they have learned and to avoid the mistakes which they are bound to make in their experiments. I sincerely hope some plan will be evolved to mark permanently that beef as No. 1 quality so that the marks will be found in the steaks and roasts as they are cut off.
It is estimated that our farmers, on account of the production of poor beef, are losing at least $10,000,000 a year on their animals as they market them. I pointed out a few minutes ago that the average weight of a carcass m the United States is about 506 pounds. I remember very well going through an abattoir in Toronto a few years ago where they were putting about 700 head) of cattle across the floor on that particular day. I was astounded to find that those carcasses weighed from about 275 to 320 pounds, indicating that they were cheap, common trash. I do not say that all1 our cattle are like that, but what I saw on that particular day impressed me most forcibly with the importance of improving the quality of our cattle. That indicates, too, hat this problem is largely in the hands of the producer, and that he must cooperate with the government in the improvement of our beef.
I have shown the great importance of the quality of our live stock. It must be remembered that we have no less than $7,000,000,000 invested in this great industry of agriculture in Canada, and if we can bring about even a small proportion of improvement in that industry, you can readily see what a great benefit that would be to the general business of the country. Under these conditions it is most surprising to me that our Minister of Agriculture and the government

have seen fit to cancel the pure-bred sire policy which was introduced in this country a few years ago, in 1913, by the Hon. Mr. Burrell, then Minister of Agriculture. That policy has rendered a most excellent service to those people who are settled in the newer parts of the country, settlers, say, in northern Ontario, in New Brunswick, or in the northern part of British Columbia, men who under ordinary circumstances would never have enough money in five years to buy a purebred sire. It was in these districts that we formed little clubs, of five or ten farmers, and sent to them a pure-bred sire. We would loan it to them for so many years, would take it to the station, pay the freight on it, and all they had to do was to take him home and give him enough to eat. After a period of five years we would find, in the first place, that the cattle in that district were very much improved, and in the second place, those ten farmers would have been educated as to the great value of the use of pure-bred stock. So the policy was rendering a splendid service to the country, and I was very much surprised to find that this year the Minister of Agriculture is proposing to eliminate entirely that policy which has been of such benefit to the cattle men of the country. I know that he is a man of high intelligence, a gentleman with a good knowledge of the live stock business, and that he appreciates the value of this policy, and why he should be eliminating it I cannot quite understand. Perhaps he has had some of the experience I had during the time I had the honour of occupying that position, when I found the greatest possible difficulty in trying to drive into the heads of the lawyers and the other men who made up the remainder of the cabinet the value of agriculture in Canada. It is strange, too, that just at this moment when the minister is proposing to eliminate this pure-bred sire policy in Canada, our friends in Ireland, our greatest competitors in the British market so far as cattle is concerned, are introducing that very policy and are going to put it into general effect.
There is another point I cannot quite understand. We will all recognize the fact that the winter fairs in this country were created for the purpose of improving the commercial live stock of the country. I remember very well when the Royal Winter Fair was started at Toronto. As minister, I had the pleasure and the honour of assisting in establishing that fair, and Toronto was selected as the most suitable place to hold the fair because it is one of the best exhibition cities in the world. The Canadian National Exhibition

Supply-Agriculture
has rendered a splendid service to this country in training our people to like exhibitions, and the result is that when an exhibition is staged in Toronto it is largely patronized by the people of that great city. The object of that winter fair, I remember very well, was to improve the quality of the commercial live stock, because we had watched the splendid results attained at the great International Live Stock Show in Chicago. Clearly that was the object in establishing the Royal Winter Fair. Now during this very session when the minister is proposing to eliminate the pure-bred sire policy, something like $35,000 a year is being offered to the Royal Winter Fair for a period of twenty years. This is simply robbing Peter to pay Paul, and in this case Peter needs the money worse than Paul does.
Before taking my seat, I want to say a word about the World's Poultry Congress which is to be held in 'the city of Ottawa during the coming summer. This congress is one of very great importance. It is a world show, and it is being held on this continent for the first time. There will be representatives here from all over the world, and I sincerely trust that 'the congress will receive the patronage of the Canadian people. The government, I understand, has dealt liberally with it, and a very excellent show should be staged. Let me point this out: We shall have here on that ocoasion representatives from all over the world interested in poultry and, no doubt, in every class of live stock, and I hope that an effort will be made to have these delegates travel clear across this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, going by one route and returning by another, so that they will have an opportunity of seeing what a wonderful country this is and what great opportunities it offers for settlement. Some people think that chickens do not amount to very much. I would1 just like to point out what one little three-pound hen has done for the province of British Columbia. This was a hen bred at the University of British Columbia, and entered at the egg-laying contest at Agassiz farm last year, the Dominion farm, so she was under Dominion supervision. This hen produced in 365 days 351 eggs. Hon. gentlemen will realize what a wonderful record that was when I say that the average biddy in Canada produces only 86 eggs per year. They have refused over $1,000 cash for this hen. Her stock is already booked for sale in 1927 to the amount of $1,275, and they have other inquiries pending to the amount of $1,000 more. It required two stenographers to answer the
correspondence with regard to this particular hen for some length of time after this record was made and had had time to reach out to different parts of the world. Inquiries came from Africa, from all parts of Europe, Asia, the United States and other parts of the world. Now if that one hen has done so much to advertise the province of British Columbia, hon. gentlemen can get some idea of what this wonderful poultry congress can do for Canada if only it is handled right.

Would the
minister tell the committee what the annual grant for the Maritime Winter Fair and Live Stock Show held at Amherst, Nova Scotia, amounts to, that is, what amount is to be allotted this year, and also the amount' allotted last year? The reason I ask this question is that last year there was a provincial exhibition held at Amherst as well as the Maritime Winter Fair and Live Stock Show, and I would like to know if the minister would feel inclined to grant the same amount this year to the Winter Fair and Live Stock Show as was granted to the two exhibitions last year, as this year I am told only one show is to be held; they are not having the provincial exhibition.

My hon. friend, I
presume, knows the story of the Amherst fair, of how they struggled along for some time with old and inadequate buildings. Inasmuch as it is the only winter fair, I think, in *the maritimes, it was felt that it was really a rallying point for the live stock industry of the three maritime provinces, and consequently we are giving them a special grant. These grants, of course, are very dangerous things to start, because you never know where you are going to get off at, but, and this is in line with the remarks I made a few moments ago, we did not know what was going to be done in connection with the Duncan report', and so we adopted a policy of reasonable generosity towards the maritimes so far as my department is concerned, and here is one of the evidences of it. This winter fair at Amherst is getting $7,000 a year; there is no specified period during which the grant will be continued, but that is $2,000 more than the ordinary grant given to the regular summer fair.

I am glad indeed to know that the minister is giving special consideration to this important show. I may say that it has been in operation for twenty-seven years, except for a period during the war, and it certainly has made great strides in the standardization and scientific breeding and raising of fat cattle for commercial purposes in the maritime provinces. The attitude of
Supply-Agriculture

the government in increasing the amount for the maritime winter fair will, I can assure the minister, be deeply appreciated.

I thought, from
memory, it was $7,000. My deputy tells me it is $8,000-one better. But there is something else that we must bear in mind. Before the war Halifax had a provincial exhibition, and if they ever come back with proper buildings-and I understand they have been living in expectation of that for the last five or six years-then we will have to consider the question as to which of these two will have the federal grant for Nova Scotia. We may be able to come to some arrangement between them whereby the fair will be alternated, the same as it is between St. John and Fredericton, but as the matter stands at present, only one fair goes to the maritime provinces and sometimes there are two equal claimants. However, it is quite possible that when Halifax comes back to her former position Amherst will claim to have a vested right and will not want to give it up, and we may have to alternate between the two. I simply mention that to show that the fair at Amherst is not a fixture. Halifax is showing evidence of coming back to life after the great disaster during the war, and when that city does come back there will be a difficult question to solve.
Does this vote include a grant to the Cobourg horse show, and if so what is the amount?

That was one of the little shows that got the better of somebody's good-nature at some time, and I am going to try to get rid of it. I have nothing against the Cobourg horse show, but we have got to stop somewhere. I think the grant was given up to two years ago. Was there an exhibition last year?
Yes.

I thought it was dropped. At any rate that was a straight horse show, a fancy show and a very nice show, but I am getting away rather from the principle of giving grants to every place that has a show of some kind or other. I wish to make the exhibition grants federal in nature and stop some of them, and I am afraid we will have to discontinue that grant.
Does the minister think the encouraging of horse breeding is commendable, as well as the breeding of other live stock?

Oh, yes, it is. It was a small grant of $1,000, but we are giving

substantial grants to horse breeding through the grants to winter fairs practically from one end of the country to the other. These small shows are springing up all over the country, and we will have the same trouble in connection with all of them. There will not be a small fair in the Dominion that will not sooner or later claim a grant and unless I draw the line of demarcation somewhere between where the Dominion will stop and the province begin there will be no end of requests.

I was
interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Tolmie) when he painted the picture of improved marketing conditions and improved demands for our beef cattle in the old country. I was interested in his resume of conditions in the United States. Further in his remarks he made reference to the quality of our beef cattle in Canada and I want to deal with that point for a few moments. For fourteen years we have had a policy in Canada, wisely adopted I think, and it has been improved during the years, of loaning pure bred sires to clubs, but for some reason or other the minister has seen fit very recently to discontinue that policy. I think possibly that is of more vital importance to the cattle industry of Canada than anything else that can be done, and I regret very much that the discontinuance of this policy has been decided upon. Now that we are, on the eve of prosperity in the agricultural line, and our products are reaching markets further and further every year, with the possibility of the United States market opening up to us in the near future, I would ask the minister seriously to reconsider his decision on the sire policy that has been discontinued. We have $15,000,000 for defence, and we have a paltry $6,000,000 for agriculture. We have half a million in the estimates for house and grounds at Washington, and we have many other items in the estimates to which I could draw the attention of this House that seem to be out of all proportion to the grant which is given to the great basic industiy of this country. Nobody will deny that. We hear it every day. I think the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., was quite correct when he said that it was very hard to drive into the heads of professional men the value of agriculture. If we are' going to improve the live stock in this country in any great volume we must get back to the man who is hesitating as to whether he will go into beef cattle or into the scrub class. The policy adopted so many years ago has done


Supply-A gricultwre
more to improve the quality of live stock than all the class A and class B fairs in the country. Those are more or less superficial in their nature. I do not condemn them in any way. That is where the men with fancy cattle meet and contest for prizes. But the man who produces beef which goes into the foreign market is the man to whom the hon. member for Victoria made reference. I ask the minister again to think seriously before he decides definitely to discontinue the policy. He says he has a staff on hand, is retaining 1,400 animals, and it will take very little more to continue that policy. I can assure my hon. friend, from first-hand knowledge, especially in western Canada, that that policy is reaping more profit for the beef industry of the country than any other expenditure that has been made by us.

I intended to make a reply to the hon. member for Victoria, but he is not in the chamber. However, as the hon, member for Last Mountain referred to the same matter, I will make a statement with regard to it. I refer to the abandonment of the bull loaning policy. I do not say that that policy has not done good work, but I think we can introduce something that will do better work. Anything you can get for nothing is never appreciated. Without going into the weaknesses of the system, I am quite free in my admission of the good work that has been done and the improvement of the live stock industry under it. Nevertheless I think we can evolve a better policy.
I had my first experience of this system in Saskatchewan in 1908, when the provincial government, of which I was a member, introduced the policy of the sale of live stock, both male and female, to settlers on easy cash terms. That policy was inaugurated following two exceedingly bad years, 1907 and 1908, for the live stock industry, and it has continued to this day. What Saskatchewan has done any other province can do. Let me pay this tribute to the eastern provinces. Over fifty years ago the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and at least two of the maritimes assisted in the distribution of bulls through the agricultural societies, and they are still continuing that policy. Consequently only a small number of the provinces have been relying entirely on Dominion assistance in this respect. So far as Manitoba and Saskatchewan are concerned, we have already made tentative arrangements, particularly with Saskatchewan. Later on I expect to see the represenative of the Manitoba government when possibly we shall be able to
complete arrangements with him. The Saskatchewan government are purchasing on an average about forty bulls a year at the regular bull sales and selling them on easy terms. I had an opportunity of meeting Mr. Hamilton recently and concluded with him a tentative arrangement under which the federal government will bear half the loss up to 15 per cent incurred by the provincial authorities in the distribution of these male animals.
I freely admit that good work has been done, but there are two sides to this question. I believe we can do better work through the purchase and sale of animals in the manner I have described. Even in poverty-stricken Russia the government sold to the peasants on long-term payments the horses which they purchased from Canada. I am receiving numerous communications like the following, which is from a gentleman named James Moffat:
I am in perfect sympathy with your policy, and hope you carry it out. It is time people were trying to walk alone without being "pap fed".
That is frank, but it is the situation. Under the loan policy we have great difficulty in keeping the animal? in condition, and sometimes it takes fifty dollars to put them in good condition aftei they have been on circuit and the club has decided to discontinue operations. Let me put on Hansard a letter, a copy of which I have supplied to several members, indicating the reason why we adopted this new policy:
Ottawa, March 8, 1927.
Dear Sir:
Your representations, relative to the federal bull loaning policy, have been duly noted.
Replying, I may say that while it is freely admitted by all that a great deal of good has come out of this method of encouraging the improvement of Canadian live stock, still, I think it must be conceded that a free distribution of anything such as this, is usually unsound as a permanent policy, it being much better to adopt the wiser program of helping those who help themselves. Besides, it is generally admitted, I think, that any agricultural activity so directly related to production as this is, naturally devolves upon the provinces to take care of it, if they so desire. As an evidence that this has been so looked upon, by at least some of the provinces, might I draw your attention to the fact that in 1908 the Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture, over which I had the honour to preside, inaugurated a policy' of selling cattle to pioneer settlers who were unable to finance the undertaking themselves, on small, initial cash payments and credit term subsequent payments, which is yet in vogue.
Shortly afterwards, the adjoining provinces of Alberta and Manitoba adopted somewhat similar policies, all indicating that provinces whose conditions seemed to warrant such an
Supply-Agriculture

enterprise were prepared to take it on as a provincial duty. Indeed, the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan still operate an annual live stock train, in which they feature very prominently the advantages of using pure-bred bulls and pure-bred males generally. Carlots of stock and suitable lecturers accompany this train, making the sales as they travel from point to point.
This is educational work of a high order with the sales part conducted on a purely business basis. Since, therefore, education has always been recognized as peculiarly the prerogative of the province, what justification is there for the federal government butting into such essentially educational work as these provincial train lecturers engage in, and worse still conducting the commercial end on a gift basis, with all its obvious weaknesses, instead of on a business basis, with all its obvious strength? In addition to this, overlapping of the federal and provincial work ensues, which should be reduced to the lowest possible minimum
Further, if the western provinces, as well as New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec (the last three through the medium of agricultural societies) can engage in this worthy enterprise when necessary, it would appear quite reasonable to expect that the remaining provinces could do likewise. It is not, however, very likely that such remaining provinces will take it up as a new venture so long as the federal continues in this provincial field.
I find also in actual practice that it is very difficult to get proper amounts allocated to federal agriculture in the annual estimates so long as considerable portions of such estimates are devoted to what are admittedly provincial activities directly associated with production. For many years this department has been criticized for its overlapping policy with the provinces, and this is one more attempt on my part to remove as far as may be possible any justification of such criticism.
We have been endeavouring for some time to find some line of demarcation between provincial and federal agricultural activities, but this is not easy to define clearly. Generally speaking, those activities directly associated with production are conceded to be provincial, while the agricultural activities associated with the standardization, grading and marketing of exportable farm products, together with the health of farm animals generally, are usually conceded to be federal.
With this in view, we have been gradually dropping some distinctively provincial work, preparatory to taking up new work of a more federal or national character, also having in mind that we can more justifiably and more effectively urge for larger and more generous estimates when the expenditure is confined a nearly as possible to federal services.
In conclusion, I may say that when any one of the nine provincial departments of agriculture shows a desire to take up, resume, or continue the distribution of pure-bred cattle to farmers on an easy sales basis, the federal department null be prepared to discuss it with them, with the view of working out some mutually agreeable business policy, under which some tangible federal encouragement and cooperation could be afforded and defended.
In the meantime, the 1,400 federally loaned bulls throughout Canada will be continued in commission.
[Mr. Motherwell.!
I would appreciate it very much if you would endeavour to see these angles of the question, although it is not easy to do so, I admit, except by one who has had an opportunity to administer this work from both the provincial and the federal standpoint.
Commending these views to your very best judgment, I remain,
Yours very truly,
W. R. Motherwell.
We are not scrapping the original policy, we are simply changing it from a loaning to an easy sales policy, with the Dominion cooperating with the provinces to the extent of carrying half the loss up to 15 per cent.

The hon. minister says that
he is changing the original scheme slightly to the extent of making it to an easy sales policy. Well, let me remind the minister that although he has been good enough to give to the Royal Winter Fair at Toronto an annual grant of $30,000, he apparently proposes to take it from the agricultural industry at the rate of $100,000 a year, because the cost of this federal sire system to-day amounts to over that sum annually. He says he is ready to cooperate with the provincial governments on very easy terms. But, Mr. Chairman, I do not think the farmers throughout the Dominion will accept his proposal as readily as those of us who are anxious to see parliament prorogue. In many parts of the Dominion undoubtedly this better sire service scheme has been of great advantage to the agricultural industry. The minister admits that himself, every member of this House admits it, and yet we find to-day he has abandoned it entirely so far as his department's responsibility financially is concerned In answer to the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Maybee) the minister said he did not know there was a horse show at Cobourg last year.
How should I know? I was 'otherwise engaged at that time, and very successfully too.
I admit it, but I would remind the minister that the Cobourg horse show was very successfully staged last year, as it generally is, and it is one of the best shows in the Dominion.
Sure.

I know the minister is interested in live stock production, and this being so, surely it is not good judgment on his part to withhold the grants from the agricultural shows that are endeavouring to put on better exhibits every year, but yet have sometimes to struggle along at a loss. I think there is

Supply-A gricidture
money in the production of horses, and a horse show of the magnitude of that held at Cobourg should surely be recognized especially at a time when the department is reducing agricultural estimates to the extent of $65,000, while asking the farmers to endorse the payment of $35,000 per annum to the royal show at Toronto. We do not object to that, but when, as I say, the department is saving $65,000 in agricultural expenditures' it is hardly right to withhold consideration from horse shows. I am not speaking particularly for the province of Ontario because I know that province will not be materially affected At the present time only about fifty-two sires are maintained in Ontario while in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec-where from $20,000 to $25,000 is being withdrawn from general expenditures- there are from 300 to 330 sires being maintained. These provinces are therefore suffering in this respect to the extent to which expenditures for agricultural purposes are being curtailed, while being correspondingly generous to other departments of the industry.
My hon. friend, I know, really wants to know the facts. We should like to make a grant to Cobourg but we must cut our coat to suit the cloth, and we have not enough cloth to go round.

You are cutting the
cloth in the wrong way.

My hon. friend
from Dufferin (Mr. Rowe) is under a misapprehension regarding the alleged relationship between the grant to the winter fair at Toronto and any change that has taken place in the bull loaning policy. There is no connection whatever between the two. As a matter of fact it is now two years since the government was first committed to the grant to the Royal Winter Fair at Toronto. And let me make it clear that the grant is not to the city of Toronto, but to the live stock industry of Canada. My hon. friend represents the constituency of Dufferin: Et tu, Brute! Does he object to this money being voted for the fair at Toronto? Surely the fair must be established somewhere, and the object is to provide some place in which to house the pure-bred live stock of Canada. That is the primary object, and we believe Toronto to be the most convenient centre. I repeat, there is no relationship whatever between grants to fairs or to anything else and the policy of the department regarding sires, because before the latter policy was even thought of, two years ago next June, if my recollection serves me, an order in council
was passed committing us to the principle of granting assistance to the winter fair at Toronto. What possible connection is there between the two, and why should my hon. friend wish to misrepresent the situation and convey the suggestion that Toronto is getting something at the expense of the farmers of the country? Where could we put the buildings if not in one of the large centres? My hon. friend knows that, but I want to draw his attention to it, and I am sure he will not continue to misrepresent the situation as he has unwittingly done.

I cannot let the minister place the statement on Hansard that I am dangling anything before the people of Toronto, and I say to him that I am quite capable of looking after myself in my affairs with that city. I have not been misrepresenting the situation, and the minister has verified what I have said. He has carefully misrepresented the statement I made, when he said that I expressed the opinion that the grant should not have been given to the Royal show in the city of Toronto. Hon. members of the committee will remember that I said we had no objection to the grant being made.
But my hon. friend said that it resulted in the impoverishment of some other place.

I want to make it quite clear t'o the minister just what I did say, although I think he understands it fairly well; with his experience in parliament he does not need to have it explained to him more than twice, surely. I would be one of the last to oppose *this grant; I have been an exhibitor at the Royal show and have been interested in it since its inception; as a matter of fact, I would *have been keenly disappointed if that grant had not been made. What I did say was that the Minister of Agriculture has given this grant to the city of Toronto, and to that no member of this House has ever objected. The minister poses as a great agriculturist, and as one interested in the agriculture industry, yet he has taken from that industry $100,000 annually, which would amount t'o $2,000,000 in the next twenty years, to give to the city of Toronto, $35,000 a year for the next twenty years, a total of $700,000. I do not want to be misrepresented, but I think the people of this country will quite understand.
What does my hon. friend call that if it is not' dangling? He has mentioned it now half a dozen times.

I hope the minister will allow me to make it clear to him, because I am sure the people of Toronto will understand it quite
Supply-Agriculture

readily. They know that no member of this House has objected to this grant of 135,000 a year, and I ask the minister if he has ever received a protest from either side of the House against this grant. It does seem strange, however, after saying that this better sire scheme which has been carried on for a number of years and which has done splendid work for the live stock of this country cannot be continued, and that he must cut his cloth according to his measurements, that the minister now proposes to continue this grant of $35,000 to the Royal show in Toronto. I would not object if that grant were increased to $50,000. The minister has shown that he is interested in the large shows but that the small shows, such as the Cobourg horse show, do not' matter. That show has had a great reflection cast upon it to-day, although it is one of the best horse shows in the province of Ontario. The grant to that show has been eliminated while t'he city of Toronto is to receive a grant of $35,000 a year. I would not object, as I have already said, if that grant were increased to $50,000, because by the abandonment of this scheme which the minister has said is a splendid one, the department will be saving enough money to permit of such an increase. The minister is merely passing the buck, asking the provincial governments and the farmers to cooperate, and assuring them that he will do everything possible to make it easy for them.

Of course I know
passing the buck is quite a favourite pastime for some, but I want to tell my hon. friend that nearly twenty years ago the provincial government of which I was a member started the first policy of buying and selling live stock to farmers on small cash payments down with the balance distributed over a considerable period. Now I am suggesting to the provinces that' if they will do as Saskatchewan and Manitoba have done, and as Alberta has begun to do, the federal government will get behind them and help share the loss up to 15 per cent. Surely that should not be deprecated; it was at least good enough for the first' province to which it was offered to accept immediately.

There is just a word I would like to say. I am not a farmer or an agriculturist, but I do know that this departure from the policy heretofore followed by the department has had a very distressing effect upon the pure bred sales which have been conducted in Calgary during the last twenty years. The people of that city have heard the news of this departure with very great sorrow, because this has had a stabilizing effect upon their business by 
reason of the purchases made at spring shows by the government. I think the minister will admit that it was most advantageous, and this departure has certainly caused a great deal of surprise, because it is not felt that the alternative suggestion will be of nearly the same benefit to the community. I am not speaking with any degree of authority, of course, but I wish to represent the view expressed to me from time to time. I recently received some communications which I brought to the attention of the minister and which indicated that the effect of the announcement of the change of policy had been very injurious upon the spring pure bred sales. I thought possibly the minister might find some method by which this policy could be continued for another year, but he quite properly pointed out to me that when you do give notice at the expiration of a period such as this, there is always the same opposition to a change as there would be if the announcement were followed up immediately by the act itself. I can quite understand that. I think the sum of money saved in this way is very great and will be a loss to the industry except in a broad way with regard to the Royal show in Toronto.

Would the minister say if
class "B" fairs are receiving anything?

They are getting
the $1,500 flat.

There
is some misapprehension as to the hog grading. Would the minister give us a little outline of that work?

If my hon. friend is in Ottawa I will give him an invitation now to be an interested spectator at the coming conference. I do not know what the result will be. The packers, swine feeders and other interested parties entered into a gentleman's agreement in 1921 which resulted in a great improvement in our bacon hogs, and it would be very lamentable if anything should happen at this time in any way to interfere with this improvement. Our swine have been so improved that Canadian bacon to-day is on a parity with the best bacon sold on the British market. I shall be glad to have any suggestions as to an alternative policy which will be nearly as good, and that is the purpose of the conference.

Then the grading is
not compulsory at present?

It is compulsory
for stock yards and producers but not in the country.

Sun Life Assurance Company
Is it true that an intimation has been received from the packers to the effect that they desire to discontinue the agreement?
Yes. They wanted to discontinue it some time ago, but I prevailed upon them to continue until representatives from all the interests concerned could meet together.

Can the minister tell
us anything in regard to the demand for Canadian bacon in Great Britain, whether it is falling of! or increasing?

The demand is
splendid. Our bacon is sometimes very scarce on the British market, which is the reason for the good prices.

Does the question of
compensation for the slaughter of animals come under this vote?

No. That comes
[DOT] under item No. 46.

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms, $1,600,000.

This grant is quite large:
but I do not think it is too large. One of these experimental farms lies almost at my door, and I have had an opportunity to observe the good work which is being done.
Progress reported.
REPORT OF COMMITTEE Mr. GEORGES PARENT (Quebec West): Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to revert to the presentation of reports, and with the leave of the House to present the fourteenth report of the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

That in accordance with the recommendation contained in the fourteenth report of the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, the fees and charges paid on bill No. 307, respecting certain patents owned by Warren Brothers Company, be refunded, less the cost of printing and translation.
Motion agreed to.

That bill No. 338 for the relief of Fanny Mayer, being an unopposed divorce bill which has been reported by the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, be now read a third time, and that rule 28 be suspended in relation thereto.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, without discussing the first clause of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River, I accept it at once on behalf of the company. As to the second clause, I must object to that. Section 104 of the act of 1917 dealing with insurance, which is chapter 9 of the statutes of 1917, provides by enactment of this parliament that the participating policyholders shall be entitled to 90 per cent of the profits arising from the participating policyholders' business, which leaves to the stockholders 10 per cent. The Sun Life Company, by a by-law of its own, 'has reduced its share from ten to five per cent, and, in the bill before the House, they propose to reduce it still further to three per cent. Having reduced their share to three per cent, and leaving the remaining 97 per cent to the policyholders, they think that is fair since under the general law they are entitled to 10 per cent.
That part of the amendment of my hon. friend from Battle River which would provide that never in the future Shall the company pay over 15 per cent to their stockholders is utterly unfair, because this company, which was incorporated just before confederation paid to its shareholders in cash dividends on its subscribed stock for nearly forty years never more than 2i per cent, and frequently less than that. In that way they have accumulated as a guarantee to their policyholders over 130,000,000, which belongs to the stockholders and is the stockholders' money, and to say that at no time in the future shall they pay over 15 per cent, if this company should in the future be in a position to distribute more, is utterly unfair, and I say that this parliament should not insert such a provision on account of the forty years during which the stockholders got practically nothing.
I am not going to deal with the matter any longer. I accept the first clause, and if it is possible, Mr. Chairman, I would like you to put these clauses to the vote of the committee separately, so that we may have a separate vote upon them. If that is not possible, I will have to move in amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Battle River that the second clause of his amendment be struck out.

speechtext: I do not know whether they were or not, but they were guaranteeing the policies of this company, and receiving com-parativelv little return on their liabilities. In 1898 the" rate went up for the first time to 2J per cent, in 1910, 1.58 per cent, and in 1911, 3.75 per cent, and so on. I am not going to discuss this amendment at length, Mr. Chairman, because I think that every word I utter is preventing other private bills from getting through this House.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member has
spoken of the small percentage the company has been paying. At the same time, I understand that the total actual cash paid into this company by the shareholders was $380,000. The hon. gentleman has just stated that the company has accumulated $30,000,000 which is the property of the shareholders. It seems to me the shareholders have done pretty well.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member for
St. Lawrence-St. George has indicated his willingness to accept the first clause of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River, and has asked that the clauses be put separately. That is a matter for the committee, not the chairman, to decide.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I will not stand for the
amendment being divided, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Then I move in amendment
to strike out the second clause of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I do not want the committee to be under any misapprehension as to the dividends which this company has paid. 1 do not want to delay the committee at all, but I would like to quote from the evidence given before the royal commission on insurance in 1906, where at page 2810, of volume 4 of the evidence, Mr. Macaulay was asked this question:
Q. Then for 1893, similarly, you take interest $4,256.07 and then 6 2/3 per cent of the profits; it is only $2,046.50 this year?-A. Yes.
Then on the next page I find the following:
Q. Then in 1897 you seem to have carried down interest the same as before, $5,871.13. It is a little more, but your capital was increasing then and instead of six and two-thirds per cent of the profits you seem to have gone down to five per cent of profits declared.
A. Yes.
As the committee is so insistent on having this matter put through, I simply say that if they would read the evidence taken before this commission they would find out that they were paying fifteen per cent. I will quote from a further question put by Mr. Macaulay:
Q. Then from 1898 to 1905 inclusive the dividend has been fifteen per cent on $105,000, or $15,750 per year?-A. Yes.
And the answer is yes. It is stated very clearly many times in this evidence that the rate of dividends that were being paid over a long period of years was fifteen per cent. I am totally unable to understand how my hon. friend (Mr. Cahan) can make the statement that the dividends are sometimes at the rate of one per cent and two per cent. I am sure he is under a misapprehension or is putting the committee under a misapprehension in regard to the matter.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
A number of us are
getting tired of being lectured by hon. members on every subject, particularly by my hon. friend from Macleod.
Subamendment (Mr. Cahan) agreed to.
Amendment as amended agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Election of first board of directors.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Section 4 as amended here
was suggested by Mr. Finlayson of the department. According to the original bill passed before confederation the directors of the company must be subjects of Her Majesty. Under the general act applying to
Sun Lije Assurance Company

all other companies incorporated since 1910 the majority must be subjects of Her Majesty. Mr. Finlayson admitted to me last night that in drafting this section he made an error. He has not changed the purport of the original act. It should read:
Notwithstanding the provisions of section 0 of the said act of incorporation the board of-directors of the company may be composed, to the extent of one-third, of persons who are not subjects of Her Majesty.
Every other insurance company incorporated or licensed to do business since 1910 must have a majority of British subjects. This company having been incorporated away back in the sixties contains a section which provides that all must be British subjects. In view of the large amount of business done in the United States, the company desire to be able to appoint one or two American directors to safeguard the interests of the policyholders. Therefore I move in amendment, in order to correct that error-and I think this will be agreed to by everyone:
That all the words after the word "company" be struck out and that there be inserted in lieu thereof the words "may be composed, to the extent of one-third, of persons who are not subjects of His Majesty".

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA

Before the amendment
carries, would my hon. friends who are promoting the bill consent to this amendment which has been given me by the Superintendent of Insurance? I thought it was agreed upon with the promoters of the bill.

'Mr. CAHAN:	I am perfectly willing to

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Sections 5 to 9 inclusive agreed to.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA

I understand one section was
passed as printed. I want to suggest to my hon. friend promoting the bill to make the section read as follows:
After the close of the calendar year in which this act shall come into force the proportion of  *

At the end of "five years thereafter," I want to put in the words " not exceeding three and a half per cent," and following the words " a further period of five years," the words "not exceeding three per cent-."

The profits of the non-participating business accruing to the shareholders shall not exceed four per cent.
