John E. Russell Company

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT

speechtext:
The House in committee on Bill No. 117, respecting a patent owned by the John E. Russell Company Limited.-Mr. Chevrier- Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Term of duration extended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister
of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) is not in his seat. I should like the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) to look at the amendments.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this
bill was before the special committee it was fully discussed. The committee ruled that the principle of extending a patent was vicious, and should not be entertained unless the promoters put before the committee the condition of things which would justify the members adopting a very exceptional view. After the discussion had taken place the committee decided to pass the bill. I do not wish to enter into the details of the discussion but the committee felt that the promoters had made out their case. The amendment passed by the committee has for its object the protection of any vested interests that may have been acquired as against the patent, and they are thoroughly protected.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
I was rather struck by the fact, Mr. Chairman, that the sponsor of this bill was the member for Ottawa, who was also sponsor of the bill for the Georgian bay canal. This probably accounts for the bill being remitted to the private bills committee without discussion in order that there might be an ascertainment of the facts before any vote was taken upon it. This you will remember, Sir, was the attitude which a good many hon. members took in this House, that on the second reading of a bill it should go before the private bills committee for the facts to be investigated. In the committee the facts were ascertained and an amendment was moved that the bill should not be reported. The reasons for that amendment I will deal with shortly. I have no intention of talking out this bill because I think it can be defeated on its merits, and I hope the day will never come when I shall have to take my place here to talk out any bill if it cannot be justified , on its merits.
The purpose of this bill is t'he renewal of a patent granted to a citizen of the United States. He sold his rights to the company who are now applying for an extension of the term. The only reason given to the committee for the passing of this bill was that
during the four years of the war the company did not make sufficient profits to meet the expenditure incurred in connection with the patent. In the committee I asked the solicitor for the bill if any royalties had been paid. He answered: Yes, royalties had been paid to the inventor. I asked where the royalties came from, and he said they were paid out of dividends. Now, the only reason given by the solicitor for the renewal of the patent was that the company wished to recoup themselves for a certain sum of money they had put into the patent; but it was shown before the committee that the company had made profits during these years when the solicitor claimed no profits were made. Out of these profits, as I have said, the royalties were paid to the inventor.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
The company
had to pay the royalties whether they made ' a profit or not.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
Just a minute. Only to-day we had another patent bill before the private bills committee and it was thrown out, but that is likely to be only one of a succession of such bills because of the fact that we have already this session passed a bill for the renewal of a patent. In the bill to which I have referred renewal was asked for, although the patent would not expire for at least eight years. The promoters of that bill were asking for it on the very same grounds as the promoters of this bill, that they had received no profits during the war years and wanted to be recouped for that period.
In the private bills committee I put this question to the officer of the patent office: What is the intention of the legislation which grants a patent to an inventor? He replied: A patent is granted in order that the inventor may recoup himself, or at all events gain the profits that his invention would give him in the open market, and only to this extent should an inventor be protected. Now, in this bill it is not the inventor who is asking for a renewal of the patent but the company which purchased it. That is, it is not the inventor who is to be protected, but the company, and they are asking this parliament to grant them an extension of eight years. That. I submit, is a principle which this parliament cannot stand for. If the inventor by his genius brings out something worth while, then in all countries his right to the profits from it for a certain period is recognized. In the old country that period I believe is sixteen years, and eighteen years in the United States. It was stated in the private bills committee that on no occasion within
John E. Russell Company

memory had a patent been renewed after its expiry. If we grant this renewal to-night we are doing so in spite of the admission that was made in the private bills committee-and I am stating what is the absolute fact-that there was nothing to justify it except the loss that might have accrued to the company during the four years of the war by reason of the fact that this material was not extensively used. Let me observe here, as I said before the committee, that during that four years there was as much building of roads and as much use of concrete pipes in the west as at any time since confederation, so that if the company lost its opportunity for securing a market the fault was theirs and nobody else's. Apart altogether from that consideration, we are giving to this company the right to charge against all the municipalities of the country the increased profits which they might derive front the exercise of the privilege. Hon. gentlemen who were in the House not long ago will remember that application was made for a renewal of a patent on radio appurtenances and that application was killed on the floor of the House for the reason that it would mean a substantial loss to the citizens of Canada. It is apparent to-day that this refusal was warranted, for the price of the article in question at the present time is half what it was then. This is due to the fact that there was open competition and other companies were allowed to come in and sell to the consumers at a much lower figure. The consumers must be looked to. They are the people who will pay for the granting of this privilege and I do not think that this House can take upon itself the renewal of the license after a period of eighteen years. Surely in all conscience eighteen years is a long enough term during which any man should be allowed to exercise a privilege against all competitors. I submit that this bill should not pass and parliament should to-night register its recognition of the principle that when a patent expires, unless in the most extreme case, it should not be renewed.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: I simply wish to support what the hon. member (Mr. Glen) has said. An application for a renewal of patent-, which was thrown out, was before the private bills committee to-day and the basis of the plea was that we had granted such an extension a few weeks ago in the case of this Bill No. 117 regarding the John Russell Company.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
This is not the first application for a renewal of a patent which the private bills committee has recommended to the House. A week ago a bill

came before parliament for the renewal of the application of a Frenchman named Frigon, who asked for an extension of a patent he brought from Switzerland. He had had bad luck, had met with an accident that laid him up for two years with both legs broken, and had suffered the loss of considerable money. The private bills committee in that case saw fit- to grant the extension, and I was one of those who supported the committee. I am glad to see the chairman of the private bills committee here to-night. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) made some reference to the fact- that the member fathering this bill had also introduced the Georgian bay bill. That is a matter of coincidence. This bill went through the House last year after thorough discussion from every angle. It got its third reading here, went to the Senate, was passed there, and only failed to obtain the royal assent. Naturally in the circumstance the John E. Russell Company went on developing their business on the strength of the expectation that the patent would be renewed. The application came before the private bills committee again this year, was fully discussed in the forenoon and deferred to the afternoon, and after very careful consideration hon. gentlemen to my left agreed to an amendment to the bill. There was proposed a sa/ving clause which, I presume, is not in print at present. The bill was adopted by twenty-seven to five, a substantial majority in the committee. Surely if there is any use of a private bills committee, who give the fullest consideration to matters of this kind, their recommendations should be given every consideration. I trust that hon. members will favourably consider the bill, especially seeing that these people have put a large amount of money into the business.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: If we defeat this bill tonight will it hinder in any respect whatever the John E. Russell Company from going ahead with their business?

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
No, but it will prevent them from earning the money which the patent has cost them. The company have spent $150,000 on patterns and forms and so far they have not realized half that investment. The hon. member for Marquette said that there had been a great- development in< Manitoba during the war, necessitating the use of the material covered by the patent. Let me assure the committee that there was no such development in Ontario, particularly around Toronto, because there was no work in connection with the construction of roads.

John E. Russell Company
The amendment moved in t'he committee was agreed to by my hon. friends to the left, and why they are opposed to it to-night I do not understand. That amendment reads:
If any person since the fifth day of August, 1926, commenced to construct, manufacture, use or sell in Canada the inventions covered by the said letters patent, such firm may continue to construct, manufacture, use or sell such inventions in as full and ample a manner as if this act had not been passed.
I hope hon. members will agree to the extension of the patent. The company has not made one-quarter of the money it has spent, for the reason that there was no development during the war. Particularly was this inactivity evident in the city of Toronto and in that part of the country where the Russell people [DOT]do most of their business. Were it not for that fact I would not urge the extension of the patent, but I do trust that the committee, after the careful consideration which the private bills committee gave to the matter, will pass the bill.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
I desire to
register my protest against the passing of this bill. The patent has already run its full eighteen years, and the company asks the renewal of it for one purpose only, and that is to continue to exploit the common consumer of Canada.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has no right to make that statement. '

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: That is only another form of special privilege and it does no credit to anyone who advocates it. It is another, way of soaking the unfortunate consumer. It is in the same category as the application which was made some years ago for the renewal of a patent on radio valves. That application was opposed by hon. members in this group and the wisdom of the House in voting it down was justified: the result has been a reduction in the price of these valves from $9 to $3. That has meant a saving of millions of dollars to the people of the north American continent. This very patent was also granted in the United States. There it has expired and it has not been renewed. That should be borne in mind.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: That is because the gentleman who owned it died.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
That has
nothing to do with it. The patent ran its course and its renewal was refused; it does not matter what the reasons were.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: We are being asked to renew a patent in favour not of the man who invented the article but of a private company whose object is to soak the people. I am absolutely opposed to anything of the kind. In Great Britain the term of patents is about fourteen years and in the United States about seventeen years. In Canada it is eighteen years-longer than anywhere else. Surely eighteen years is a long enough period in which the owner of a patent, or any private company controlling it, should be allowed to exploit the public.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: As soon as the noise has subsided I might suggest to the hon. gentleman that he is quite right when he says that when an attempt was made to secure full information with respect to the condition of this company, that is, with respect to its profits, its books and accounts and so on, that information was not forthcoming. There was some general statement made which in my opinion was not satisfactory, and until the company produce more adequate proof that they deserve some consideration I fail to see why this parliament should be asked to continue a principle as vicious as that proposed in this bill. After all, our primary duty is not to represent private interests but to represent the interests of the great consuming public. If this bill is permitted to pass we may anticipate a flood of similar bills coming up for consideration, and if we once create a precedent we will have great difficulty in justifying any objection to bills of this character which may subsequently come before us. Picture it for yourself; use your own imagination and consider what is liable to happ'en if we create a precedent now for renewing these wretched patent bills after almost illimitable periods have elapsed, bills which deliberately steal from the pockets of the people that which the people can ill afford to pay.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
The John E.
Russell Company are well respected and well known, and are not asking for anything unreasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
I am not questioning the
respectability or the financial standing of the John E. Russell Company; I did not attend the meeting of the private bills committee, so I am not very well posted as to the nature of the patent. But if, as I infer, this is a patent which will enable this company to collect royalties from all the municipalities making cement pipes, I agree with the ob-

John E. Russell Company

servations made by the hon. member for Bow River. It may be that the fact that the bill passed the House last year and did not receive royal assent places those of us who were in the House last year under some obligation, but certainly not to grant this extension for eight years, and I would suggest to my hon. friend that he cut down that period considerably.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
It was cut down to eight
years last year. When this came before the committee last session and the committee went into it, they unanimously agreed that it was right to grant an extension of time, but the time requested was twelve or fourteen years. The company reduced that to eight years. This company has invested already some $150,000 on account of this patent, and because of the attitude of the House last year they have invested still more money, and they simply ask the House to complete what was done last year. The evidence convinces me that it is a fair proposition, and I think parliament should grant the extension.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
All over this country there
are small industries making sewer pipes and pipes for road drainage for the local communities. It seems to me that it is very unreasonable to put this company in a position to collect royalties from these other small companies.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
I do not think
there is any intention on the part of the John E. Russell Company to collect royalties. However, if the Minister of Finance wishes that two years be taken off the term, and the House is satisfied, we will do so..

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
I would like to suggest that
you move an amendment which will safeguard the municipalities.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
So far as we
know there are no firms making these pipes; it is an invention whereby two pipes are cemented together; it is a wonderful thing, and these people have a right to some consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Cut it down by six years.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
When the hon. member states that no one else has any interest in this business, he is stating what is not according to the evidence given before the private bills committee. A representative of the Dominion Sewer Pipe Company appeared before that committee and stated that they were about to manufacture these concrete pipes, that they had already purchased a site for which they had paid $15,COO in cash, on which

they were to manufacture concrete pipes. When my friend says there was no opposition to it, he is also wrong; opposition was expressed right in the committee.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: This year, but not last year.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: The length of time is not the question at all; the question is whether this House shall decide upon a principle of renewing patents which have expired for a good many years, and whether this House is prepared to sanction that as a rule by which to be guided in the future.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Marquette has stated what I was about to say. It is a fact that last year this bill passed through the committee without opposition but this year encountered strong opposition, and that fact alone is sufficient to warrant us in departing from the position taken a year ago.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
I do not happen to be
on the private bills committee, and of this House there are perhaps 215 members who were not present at that meeting and who are not aware of all the circumstances connected with this patent. That is so in the case of ah private bills, and one who is not on the committee must trust to the findings of the committee in these matters. We did not hear the evidence but we have the report, in which we are informed that this committee, while it unanimously passed this bill last year, passed it on this occasion by a vote of 27 in favour with 5 against. The only safe course for those who were not present at the meeting and who did not hear the discussion, I think, is to follow the report of the committee under these circumstances. That is a rule which has been laid down for many years in this House and it is a rule which I propose to follow tonight.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Would the leader of the opposition consider this position, that the statements which have been made in opposition to the bill have not been denied and cannot be denied by any hon. member of this House? If these statements are correct, surely it is for the House to decide and not for the committee, as to whether we shall establish such a principle?

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
I have been very much interested in the discussion and the arguments put forward by some hon. members to my right in giving their reasons why this bill should go through. One argument is that it went through the committee last year. I would like to remind hon. members that the

Sun Life Assurance Company
Georgian bay canal bill went through this House thirteen times, and those who opposed it most- strenuously this year were the hon. members to my right. I think they were right in so doing. Another argument advanced is that the bill we are now considering went through the committee this year with a vote of 27 to 5, so we are told. I want to tell the committee that there was no vote counited at all, and as one of the minority I know that more than five voted against it.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: The hour for private bills having expired, I now resume the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: If we might have the unanimous consent of the House, Mr. Speaker, there are some bills which have been held up, and the government offer no objection to continuing for at least another hour. I think we were committed to that by some hon. gentlemen opposite, but we are entirely in the hands of the House since it must be by unanimous consent.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext:
May I ask a question on
that point? Will the Minister of Finance give us any assurance as to when the House will rise to-night if we permit this suggestion? Last night we sat until half past two, after a late session the ni^ht before-

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: My hon. friend is making a mistake; it is not a question of consent but a matter to be agreed upon among the members of the House in order to expedite business. We do not want to rush anything.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: There is no motion before the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: I did not make any motion. I said that the government offered no objection to continuing another half hour or hour in committee on private bills if the House was unanimous in regard to the matter.

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Am I to understand that it is the judgment of the House that it should resolve itself into committee of the whole on private bills for another half hour? By unanimous consent?

maintopic: JOHN E. HUSSELL COMPANY, LIMITED, PATENT
speechtext: Carried.

That it is urgent that Bill No. 107, respecting the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada (as amended), be now read a third time, because private bills will not be placed on the

The House in committee on Bill No. 237, to incorporate the Red River Driving Club- Mr. Beaulbien-Mr. Johnston 'in the chair.

I wish to oppose the
further progress of this bill. The object is to incorporate a racing club in the city of St. Boniface, and as I come from that city I am interested in the proposal. I was not in the House when the bill was referred to the private bills committee or I would have opposed that motion. In the province of Manitoba we have six racing clubs to-day, there being three race tracks in greater Winnipeg. Provincial legislation provides for a week's racing in each of the spring and fall meets, and as a matter of fact it is impossible for three or four of the six clubs in Manitoba to stage any events at all. The men behind this bill are seeking to circumvent the laws of the province of Manitoba and to carry on racing there and in other provinces west in spite of provincial legislation. The purpose of the bill is not to provide racing in the true sense of the word; it is not to encourage the (purely sporting spirit. The purpose is to enable the incorporators to use the pari-mutuel machines in order to transfer sums of money from the pockets of citizens to their own. If the parimutuel privilege were removed from the bill this measure would fail flat. The business interests of Winnipeg, the citizens themselves, and the legislature of the province of Manitoba are all opposed to it. I have received from the Attorney General of Manitoba the following telegram:
Have wired Premier King as follows: "Today's newspapers item states Red River Driving Club, Bill No. 237, reported from private bills committee of House of Commons. The government of Manitoba submits that already there are sufficient tracks in Manitoba to accommodate the public requirement for horse racing. The holding of numerous race meets in Manitoba became a serious evil and the Manitoba legislature after careful consideration enacted the Horse Racing Regulation Act in 1926. Any increase in present number of associations which have power to hold race meets makes the situation more difficult to handle. Government of Manitoba therefore submits that your parliament should not pass this bill. Am confident Manitoba legislature would not pass similar bill." Would appreciate your opposition to this bill.
There are also telegrams from the board of trade and other prominent corporations in the city oif Winnipeg opposing this bill. There is ample provision for racing in Manitoba at the present time. We have four weeks of racing every summer as well as race meets on the ice two days in every week of winter. It is becoming a serious problem for the local legislature to deal with and I wish to protest against the progress of the bill. If in order, I beg to move that Bill No. 237, to incorporate the Red River Driving Club, shall not now be proceeded with but that it be referred back to the special committee on miscellaneous private bills for reconsideration.

This legislation is wholly provincial in character and in the ordinary course of events it should not be before this House at all'. The Solicitor General might advise us whether or not, in his opinion, it should be considered by this parliament. Its objects are purely provincial, it incorporates a body which will function withini the province, and it does not touch any other province. The bill should be considered by the legislature and not by this parliament.

private bills committee that the corporation intended doing business in other provinces and that brought it within the federal scope.
No,
I want to correct my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett). The object of the bill is to enable the corporation to circumvent provincial laws.

West Calgary has pointed out, these bills are generally submitted1 to (the provincial legislatures. I do not think that this parliament
The Sealright Company

Before the item carries I should like to make a statement with regard to the experimental farm in Ottawa. I have spent considerable time at the experimental farm since coming here, and I have
found that there is not nearly enough land there to carry on the work of the farm properly. I think that in this House we are not voting nearly enough money for agriculture. Agriculture is responsible for the employment of over 'half the people of Canada, feeds all of them, and we vote only $6,000,000 for it in our estimates. At the experimental farm in Ottawa we are using for field crops only about 120 acres all told. That is not nearly enough to do the work that should be done by the experimenters there. For instance, the animal husbandry department has only 23 acres, and they have over 200 head of cattle for dairy purposes, 100 head of beef cattle, over 150 head of swine and a great many sheep to look after. Practically every department at the experimental farm is over-crowded, and proper work cannot be done. The work at the experimental farm has been responsible for enriching the Dominion of Canada by hundreds of millions of dollars in the last few years, because they have been able to find new kinds of grain, new kinds of fruit and by breeding and selection to improve all kinds of farm animals. The House should seriously consider, at least another year, the buying of more land adjacent to the farm at Ottawa. I think that members of parliament, the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister should know that adjacent to the experimental farm at Indian Head, Saskatchewan, a man named William Patterson has lived for a great many years on a beautiful section of land. He has good buildings, good stock and machinery. Mr. Patterson has turned over to the Dominion government that entire piece of land, with all equipment, at a rental of $1,000 a year, and is providing that upon his death it shall revert to the government, free, for experimental purposes. He has seen the work that has been carried on at the experimental farm and has been so strongly impressed by it that, as I say, he is leaving his entire fortune in the shape of a section of land in Saskatchewan, worth at least $100 per acre, to the government. I think the government and the House of Commons should in some way recognize the gift of Mr. Patterson of Indian Head.

It is recognized that this procedure is a considerable advance over methods which have been advocated and experimented upon up to the present time. The work of the Alberta committee on this vaccine is, as far as is known, the most extensive in Canada.
I might say also that both in Great Britain and the United States they are recognizing that a vaccine can be developed that will play a very important part in this work. I quote from an article on the prevention of tuberculosis in cattle by Nathan Raw, C.M.G., M.D, M.P., a member of the British House of Commons.
It is estimated that a million dairy cows in Great Britain are at present affected with tuberculosis, of which about five per cent are affected in the udder, rendering these cows extremely dangerous to the public health.
If all these cattle were destroyed to-morrow, and full compensation given to the owners, it would not solve the problem, as another generation of calves is coming on, many of them already infected, either by living in contact with their mothers, or infected in the early weeks or months of life by drinking the milk of a tuberculous cow.
The only solution to the problem is prevention of infection.
Then we have a memorandum from Doctor W. C. White, of Washington. I am not going to weary the committee by reading all of this long letter, but they are proceeding very much on the same principle as we are in Canada, that is slaughter and -compensation. He says:

In cattle I believe the process will be by vaccination and by pasteurization of food products and not by the fearfully wasteful method of condemnation and destruction of the present time.
I ask the minister just what work they are doing across the river at Hull, in regard to this research investigation, and what success they are having. Is he doing any practical work with animals or just laboratory work?

I have already
given, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Kingston, a list of the research work, or nearly the whole of the research work. We have two stables over in Hull pretty well filled with live animals, calves, grown cows and guinea pigs, and so on. I think it would be worth my hon. friend's while to go over there and see it, because it is very interesting. When we get through the seven restricted areas with three of them with less than one per cent of reactors in the first test we are persuaded it is not so expensive a method as it would be in the old country and is in the United States. In the case of Prince Edward Island, Last Mountain in Saskatchewan and the small area in New Brunswick, the reactors on first test all came below one per cent. The time to get the disease is when it is in the early stages. If my hon. friend has any better method we should like to know it. We hope to develop a vaccine in the new laboratory that will act as a preventive, so doing away with the necessity for adopting the slaughter cure. I believe in time we will be able t'o get good results, but this Calmette vaccine has not as yet attained that end. No veterinarian will advocate that as a cure. The best they will do is to say that it may benefit for a year or two, but that is not' satisfactory. The research workers are coming nearer the solution all the time. In the meantime we are making use of the best methods that are at our disposal to cope with this matter.

I would like to draw the
attention of the minister to the fact that in my constituency we are concerned with t'he important high class breeding animals, although we are not a dairying country. Our breeders complain that the embargo placed on the importation of breeding cattle from Scotland and England is too rigid. That' embargo was put in force owing to the fact that in England a few years ago there was an outbreak of the foot and mouth disease. In England they isolated the sections in which the disease existed. Last month this restriction was lifted, because in England and in Scotland

they considered that there was no danger of the spread of the disease over there. I am told by the department here that' unless six months have elapsed after an outbreak from any cause in the old country they will not permit high-class cattle to be brought from England to Canada. It is a rule of this department not to permit the importation of domestic live stock from any country where the foot and mouth disease exists until sixty days have elapsed after an outbreak.

I cannot allow this
opportunity to pass, even though it is late, without making a few remarks to the minister.
I am heartily in accord with this restricted area development throughout Canada, and it is especially important to the section I am interested in, because already the department has an area reaching between the American boundary and the St. Lawrence river as far as the Richelieu river, which is now a practically clean area. Part of this vote

Mr. Chairman, I think

Some time ago I asked the
minister for information regarding compensation paid to one Andrew Oberle of Walker-ton, Ontario, for the Slaughter of swine. I received the papers only to-day, and as they comprise a bundle of 182 pages it has been almost impossible for me to peruse them closely. I notice, however, that the deputy minister on December 3, 1925, wrote to Oberle saying that he and the minister both felt that the department was under no obligation whatever except for the price of sixteen hogs which had been killed by mistake by the inspector, and therefore if he did not accept a cheque for $240 the account would be closed. On the following day a cheque for this amount was sent to Oberle. But I find that on February 24 of this year an order in council was passed to compensate him to the extent of $1,910. Under whose recommendation was this order in council passed?

The responsibility
for paying that was placed upon me by the House. It appeared in the estimates just the same as a number of small payments appear this year in the main estimates and in the supplementaries. These items cannot be paid under the law because the animals sometimes die on the way to be slaughtered. We changed our decision after reviewing the case. As the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., knows, there are mild types of hog cholera which one man will diagnose as such, while another will be of opinion that it is not hog cholera. This case became more complicated by the local authorities calling in veterinarians, and Dr. McGillivray of Guelph College diagnosed the trouble as cholera. But our men did not so diagnose it. When veterinarians differ our policy is to give the man who suffers the loss the benefit of the doubt.

I do not think the minister
has made the case clear in view of much of the evidence that I find in this file. It seems rather strange that Oberle lost so many hogs. He is an experienced hog dealer and feeder, and prior to any inspector from the depart-

ment visiting his farm he had lost one hundred hogs that had not been reported to the department at- all. That, I understand, was berore May 1 last year. There is no doubt that he had been turning over a large number of hogs because on June 12 an inspector found 260 hogs on his farm. On June 25 the department received a telegram asking that an inspector be sent to the farm and that he, Oberle, had only 20 hogs left out of 300. On June 29 we find an inspector arrived and found 283. Mr. Nichols, the inspector, slaughtered a couple of hogs and later another hog to ascertain the trouble, and he was absolutely convinced there was no evidence of hog cholera, after sending the carcasses to headquarters for examination. The inspector visited the farm on July 19 and found only 16 hogs there. Oberle had lost 47 hogs in one interval and 49 in the other. Oberle was doing an extensive business and none of the hogs were kept on the farm very long. The inspector's report shows that Oberle purchased from fourteen different farmers, and the investigation demonstrated that none of those farmers' hogs were infected. During all this time Oberle was allowed to ship hogs, and he sold 182 and another shipment of 142 to the packing houses in Toronto. No quarantine was imposed on his farm. Everyone who understands anything about such a fatal disease as hog cholera will realize that if these hogs were not in quarantine some other farmers in the district would have had their animals infected. But we find that Mr. Oberle continued to conduct his business. The veterinary director general in his report stated that had Mr. Oberle followed the advice of Mr. Nichols he would have.lost scarcely any hogs. The fault was due to improper feeding; he was giving the hogs tankage, slaughterhouse offal and buttermilk which was altogether unfit for them. It is rather strange that the district inspector, Mr. Watson the chief pathologist, Doctor Hilton, the veterinary director general and others, being of the opinion that there was absolutely no sign of cholera, the department should have undergone such a change of heart as to pay $1,910 instead of $240 which they had agreed upon long before. The minister says that there were evidences of hog cholera, but according to his letter he forwarded the cheque of $250 as payment in full for the sixteen hogs that were killed in error. He admits that there was no cholera, because, if there was, why should he pay $250 "in full"? Under the Animals Contagious Diseases Act, wherever cholera is evident only two-thirds of the value of the animals slaughtered is paid, whereas in

this case the full value is given. It will readily be admitted that $15.60 on an average for 115 hogs is a good price for such animals as these. The department paid not only for sixteen hogs which admittedly should not have been killed, hogs that had no cholera, but there were ninety-six more that died and were paid for. I remember the Minister of Agriculture making the unconsciously humorous statement last year that these hogs had "all died on the road to death". Well, it seems they were a long time on the road to death, because they were dying all the way from June 12 to September 1. The minister declared that the reason the department paid for these hogs was that they had died before they could be slaughtered. If they died before they could be slaughtered it is evident that the department paid for hogs which the inspectors never saw. These hogs went to the dealer who was turning over hundreds of animals per month. Sometimes he would handle as many as 400. The act provides that no owner shall be reimbursed unless the hogs are slaughtered by order of one of the inspectors, but here we find ninety-six hogs being paid for in full although the inspector had never seen them. The inspector had only the word of the dealer that the hogs had died before they reached his place.
I cannot understand how the minister can claim that the hogs were suffering from cholera, because he knows that no such report was made by the inspector. The chief inspector of Ontario, the veterinary director general, and the pathologist took five of these hogs from Walkerton and examined them at headquarters and their report was that the hogs were not in good condition. They were not thrifty, there being evidence of undernourishment. They inoculated one hog with the blood of another to see whether cholera was present and they failed to infect any of these five animals. One of them died from pneumonia, and it was only after the other four had been inoculated with cholera germs that they succumbed. It was no wonder therefore that Mr. Watson reported no signs of hog cholera in these animals. They even brought three new experimental hogs and injected into them the blood from the hogs taken from Walkerton, and they failed to infect any of these three with cholera. Nevertheless, in face of all these experiments which could not reveal one trace of cholera, we find the department paying not only for the sixteen animals slaughtered by mistake, but for ninety-five others which the inspector never saw.
Yes, there was one.
The minister owes the committee an explanation.

I have given one.
My hon. friend seems to think there is something strange about the matter.

There is something
strange.

There is nothing strange about two diagnoses about the same trouble. Someone has to decide and we made the best decision we could. We had the agricultural college of the Ontario government on the side of one of our veterinarians, while there were two other veterinarians on the other side, and we arrived at the soundest decision possible in the light of all the circumstances. Where there is any doubt in a matter of this kind the preference is always given to the man whose property is at stake. My hon. friend has played baseball and he knows that in a doubtful decision the base runner gets the preference. I do not see anything strange about it.

I appreciate the minister's explanation: and I think his reference to baseball is rather appropriate. In this instance Mr. Oberle was playing shortstop, because so far as I can see he has got favours which nobody else has enjoyed. While there was a difference of opinion I do not think that the payment for all these hogs can be justified. I would not criticize the minister for paying for the sixteen hogs slaughtered by mistake. It was purely a mistake, as the minister admits. The deputy minister acknowledges that too, as do the chief pathologist and the veterinary director general. No one would be so critical as to find very much fault over a mistake. At the same time it is difficult to understand why the department should pay for ninety-five hogs which there is not the slightest evidence to show had been inspected. We have not the slightest trace of any evidence that the inspector had looked at one of them. The minister will not deny that forty-seven of them died between June 12 and June 29, not one of them having been seen by the inspector; and between June 29 and July 14, when Inspector Tennant visited the farm, forty-nine more had died. Besides these there were three which Inspector Nichols killed and sixteen Inspector Tennant had slaughtered by mistake, making 115 in all. I contend that only 19 of these 115 hogs could properly have been paid for under the Contagious Diseases Act. The minister has not explained it at all, because I have not noticed in the 182 pages of evidence any mention that the inspector saw

I did not intend to hold up this estimate for so long, Mr. Chairman, but in view of the explanation made by the minister the committee might be interested in hearing a letter written from the Veterinary Director General to the deputy minister, under date of May 27, 1926, which is as follows:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 21st, instant, enclosing copy of a claim made by Mr. Andrew Oberle regarding compensation for fatalities among his hogs.
In reply to your request in this connection I desire to first point out that Mr. Oberle shows in his statement of claim approximately one hundred more fatalities than those reported by our officers, and which I outlined in my letter to you of April 30, last.
Special measures were taken .in this case in an endeavour to demonstrate the existence of hog cholera infection, with negative results. The premises were not maintained under quarantine and still the disease did not spread through the district. I am consequently not in a position to change my opinion, which has been expressed on more than one occasion.
The act which I am administering makes no provision for paying compensation for animals dying from diseases which it purports to control.
The sole object of the act is to control diseases which are a menace to our live stock, and provision is only made for paying compensation for animals ordered slaughtered by our officers for the protection of other live stock owners. I am, therefore, of the opinion that Mr. Oberle will be receiving fair treatment in the circumstances if he is paid the full value of the sixteen hogs slaughtered by Inspector Tennant and for the three slaughtered for post mortem purposes by Inspector Nicholls. This would involve a payment of $270.

I would like to ask the minister a question with regard to the inspection of seed potatoes and potatoes of grade A. We find that when a farmer is selling a carload of certified seed potatoes and he gets an inspector to give him a certificate covering the grade of those potatoes, he does not pay anything; the service is free. But if the same farmer or his neighbour is selling a carload of grade A potatoes and he wants a certificate covering the grade of those, he has to pay $5 a ear for the inspection certificate. It seems hardly fair that the man who is getting the higher price for the certified seed potatoes should go scotJfree, white the man who is selling grade A stock and getting the lower price has to pay a fee for the inspection certificate. I would like to suggest that both farmers should be put on the same basis in this respect. Has the minister ever considered this matter?

We want to encourage the production of certified seed! because it is a very valuable commodity. It is one of the chief sources of revenue from not only Prince Edward Island but the maritimes generally. If you are going to sell potatoes abroad in Virginia or elsewhere as certified seed potatoes, you must have them inspected and the government's certificate for them. That is obligatory and no fee is charged. The other is a purely commercial transaction. The potatoes are not. what we call certified seed; they are table stock. The owners of this

stock want to sell their goods abroad, and the only way in which they can sell them to the best advantage is by having somebody examine them, see that they are of uniform variety1- usually white is in the best demand-and that they have the government's certificate behind them. Those people are ready and offer to pay $5 a car for that service. The certificate is worth many times $5 to them for putting their goods on the market. We had requests from so many places in the maritimes for inspectors that we were not able to pick up enough men there for the work. This inspection is optional.
Mr. MA'CDONAjLD (Kings): First of all I do not consider the explanation at all logical, and further I should like to criticize very strongly the action of the department in that regard. In the first days of December last in Prince Edward Island every inspector with the exception of one to the east of Charlottetown went out of service and any dealer who had an order for a carload of potatoes loaded east of Charlottetown had to get an inspector from Charlottetown. The result was that orders had to be turned down because inspectors could not be secured. The trouble was not the matter of the $5 inspection fee, although I maintain there should not be such a discrimination between the growers. This is the situation. A farmer goes to work and grows, say a ten acre field of seed potatoes under inspection from certified seed, and he intends to sell them as certified seed. If he succeeds in passing all the inspection and his stock is all right, he gets the inspection certificate when he loads the stock on to the car, and his bags are tagged. This service costs him nothing. But supposing his stock fails to pass inspection, he will probably get 25 cents a bushel less for the stock and then he has to pay $5 for having it inspected. That is not fair.
Then there is the other feature. In December, January and' February last, inspection could not be secured at all with the result that farmers or dealers wanting to sell carloads of table stock had to refuse orders which demanded inspection. With the situation as it is in Kings county, Prince Edward Island, where there is one train a day, how is one inspector from the centre of the province in Charlottetown going to serve the whole of the eastern part of that province. The situation is absolutely absurd. It puts out of business the people who want to sell potatoes under inspection. If they have orders for any grade of potatoes, they can not secure the inspection and consequently they have to turn down the orders. This is an important matter
[Mr. Motherwell.)
in Prince Edward Island and I would certainly very strongly urge the minister to give it his serious consideration.

I am very glad
there has been such a land office demand for these inspectors that we have not been able to supply my hon. friend with them in sufficient numbers. If we are going to put them in there with the speed with which he would like to have them, he must expect to pay something for their service because we do not pick them up for nothing. I do not understand the minister and I cannot see how any other hon. member can understand him. I am not objecting to have the certified seed inspection free.
But the hon. member is pleading for equality of treatment.

The man
who is receiving the lower price for his product should not be charged an inspection fee when the man who receives the higher price is not so charged. I am a little
interested in this service to which my hon. friend from Kings refers. So far as the service which was given last year for the inspection of table stock is concerned, it was fairly satisfactory. At one period of the season when the large shipments were taking place before navigation closed, there were twelve inspectors at the service of the shippers in Prince Edward Island. When the middle of December came, eight of these inspectors were let out, but they were still always available for service from day to day if required, and were used by the day at times when they were required during the balance of the season. The inspectors were chosen from each of three counties, at least two from each county, which would make six, and the others were chosen from where they could best be secured for the purpose.
In regard to the cost of the inspection I may say that I and my colleague from Queens were waited on by shippers in Prince Edward Island in the early part of October, and were asked to try to provide this service. The shippers of potatoes particularly were desirous of having this service, and they themselves offered to pay a reasonable fee. The fee charged previous to that time was $5 a car when the certificate was given by the inspector. Before last year we were only in a position to inspect a few care. Some were inspected before they went aboard the ferry, but during the last season most of the inspection was done where the care were loaded, which was a more satisfactory inspection.
I think it would be a mistake to urge the minister to make a charge for the inspection of seed stock or for certifying seed potatoes. When you inspect potatoes for certification, you must inspect the growing crop twice during the season; you must also inspect the tuber after it is put in the pile, after the pile sweats, as it is termed, and later you must inspect the potatoes when they are in the bags ready for shipment before the tag is put on them. So it involves a series of inspections, and it is proving worth while
not only to our people in the east but to Canada as a whole, because we have a growing industry in the producing of certified seed which is shipped to the United States, and which helps in a large measure to make favourable to Canada the balance of trade between Canada and the United States. It is a business to which I feel the Department of Agriculture should give every attention, and I do ask the minister not to think of making a charge at this time for the inspection of certified seed, because that is a growing industry and one that will mean a great deal to the maritime provinces and the eastern part of the province of Quebec, which is really the territory in Canada that will in the future supply seed potatoes for the southern growers.

I do not

I do not know whether any more mad proposal was ever brought before this House than was brought forward last year by one of the front benchers on the Conservative side that the coal should be shipped lake and rail. No one knows better than those of us who live in Alberta that while our coal is of a domestic quality fully equal to any other used in this country, it will not stand harsh handling. One or two handlings are the most that it will stand without serious deterioration. I submit therefore that this vote is practically worthless and I venture to predict that not one dollar of it will ever be used. I venture to assert further that not a single operator in Alberta would prejudice the possible market for his coal by consenting to have it moved by lake and rail. Our operators know too well the danger of putting this coal down chutes into the hold of a vessel, hauling it out again with great clamshells and dropping it on the dock. The coal will not stand that treatment, but it will stand reasonable handling in box cars all rail. This morning we had a brief discussion in regard to the coal miners in Alberta. If the minister had the interest of the miners at heart-and I really think he has, but possibly officials of his department are leading him off into little highways and byways on other questions instead of letting him go ahead in the direction in which I feel sure he wants to go-he would have devoted this $15,000 to assisting the movement by rail until the Board of Railway Commissioners had reported on the cost rate. In that way the minister would have done infinitely more good to Alberta in the marketing of our coal than he will do by this vote in connection with the lake and rai. shipment of it.

Has the Department of Justice done anything towards carrying out the resolution which the House passed last year to provide that prisoners should be given a sufficient amount of productive work to do to help towards keeping their dependents.

When my hon. friend moved her resolution in the House last year, the hon. Minister of Justice stated he would endeavour to carry it out to the best of his ability. I understand he has taken steps in that direction, but unfortunately, as my hon. friend will understand, I am not in a position to give her any details. I have been called upon to present these estimates to the House, but I am not as fully conversant with them as the Minister of Justice would be. I am quite sure, however, from the knowledge I have acquired in the department that the Minister of Justice has done his best to improve the situation in the direction the hon. member outlined last year.

I believe that the act as it stands is drawn up on the old idea of vengeance by the state, and in view of that fact I think that the wardens and other officials of the penitentiary are doing most excellent work. Certainly in the penitentiary I visited I was very much impressed with their efficiency. I think the wardens, the matrons, the guards, and the officials in charge of the prisoners are doing everything they can to change-shall I say distort?-the meaning of the act and to reform rather than to revenge, using punishment only in so far as it will help in reformation. I do think that the act should be revised to express the new spirit that is to be found to some extent in the penitentiaries. In the report which the superintendent of penitentiaries makes every year, he asks for certain things. He has made certain recommendations over and over again, and I hope that the Department of Justice will endeavour to carry them out. Brigadier-General Hughes is most interested in this subject. He devotes his whole time and energy and all his reading and thought to it. He has made certain specific recommendations for many years past, but they have not been carried out. I cannot see the force of having a man who is to advise the government if the government does not take his advice. These recommendations which he has made over and over again are very important. There are some seven or eight of them. One is that prisoners be given a sufficient amount of work to do, and get paid for work well done. He also asks that the officials in the penitentiaries, the guards 32649-151
and all who take charge of the prisoners, shall have training before they go there, and another one which I forget at the moment; but I would refer the minister who is putting these estimates through to the report of the superintendent of penitentiaries, and most respectfully suggest to him and the government that they should carry out the recommendations made yearly by Brigadier-General Hughes.

To complete the revision of the Dominion statutes; payments may be made notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act or regulations thereunder, $20,000.
When will these statutes be completed?

The commission was to complete its work by the 1st of January last. In the fall when I was Acting Minister of Justice I had a conference with the commissioners and they pointed out that in view of the fact that practically no legislation was passed last year, if the revision were completed by the end of this year we would be in the rather abnormal position of having a revision which would be minus very important legislation, and they suggested that they should be continued in office, in order to be in a position to include in the revision legislation which would be passed this session.
Why not go on forever?

Allow me to finish. Take, for instance, the amendments brought in by last year's budget or this year's budget, the Pension Act, and all these important pieces of legislation: I do not think it would be fair to the commission to ask them to terminate their work without including the measures we pass this session. The hon. member for West Calgary and the leader of the opposition will admit that it is in the public interest, and

Supply-Justice

also in the interests of the bar, that we should include in our revisions the legislation of this year, and I have the assurance from the commissioners that they will be able to complete their work in a very short time. I asked them if it would be possible to finish by July 1, and they told me they would endeavour to do so, I can assure the House that their work will be finished within a very short time.

There are two things I have despaired of, one is the revision of the [DOT] Dominion statutes and the other is a solution of the question as regards Alberta coal. The Dominion statutes were last revised in 1906. I remember that in 1921 a very able lawyer offered to do the whole job in one year for $10,000. The offer was accepted, but subsequently it was set aside by another government. This commission has been working ever since. They are paid an annual salary.
What is the cost?
I do not know the total cost, up to the present time.
What has been the total cost up to date?
Who is the president of the revising board?

Sir Charles Fitzpatrick,
former Chief Justice of Canada.

Item agreed to.
Justice-salaries-to provide for the appointment of Antonio Berthiaume as clerk, grade 4, in the minister's office, $1,500.
To provide for the salary of a stenographer, grade 2, $1,020.	_
To provide for promotion of a clerk, grade 2 to clerk, grade 3, $120.
To raise the salary of one senior advisory counsel, $4,620 to $5,000, $380.
Can the Acting Minister of Justice justify the additional appointments to the staff?
The staff of the Justice department is a very small one. It is the only department which is really under-manned.

They are all over-manned.
. Mr. KENNEDY: Why is it necessary to have increased salaries for stenographers and clerks? Why do they not come under the Civil Service Commission?

They do. The stenographer in this item belongs to the Penitentiaries branch and after two years' temporary service was made permanent last year, the salary

having been included in the general items of promotion from classification. Owing to the delay in passing the supplementaries for 192627 the salary was omitted when the main estimates for 1927-28 were considered. All these classifications and increases are statutory.

Item agreed to.
To provide increase of $3,000 per annum for Hon. Lucien Cannon, payable to him from the consolidated revenue fund, for the period during which he occupies the position of Solicitor General, the acceptance of such salary not to vacate his seat in parliament, $3,000.
Explain.

I am not going to deal
with that item. Someone else will attend to that.

The Solicitor General
will not misunderstand me when I say that it should be a matter of policy, so far as the government is concerned, that both law officers of the crown should not come from a civil law province. There should be one from a common law province and one from a civil law province. I have always felt that. In the previous adminstration with which I was connected1 it was not so, but that made it no better. As far as the item is concerned, if the Solicitor General of this country is charged with the same duties as the Solicitor General in England with respect to litigation,-and I believe that is the intention here-the compensation at present paid to him is wholly inadequate and he should be put on a higher basis. In England the Solicitor General undertakes a great deal of the civil litigation, and sometimes undertakes criminal prosecutions, but only in very important cares. In addition to his salary he is paid for the work he undertakes by the solicitor of the treasury endorsing on his brief a fee exactly the same as would be paid to other lawyers who might be called in. The idea of increasing the salary to $10,000 if the work is done is not at all paying the Solicitor General more than he should receive. As long as he undertakes this work I think he should be paid this salary. However, as I said, I think one of the law officers should come from a common law province and one from a civil law province.

Item agreed to.
Supreme Court of Canada-To provide for portraits of chief justices, $1,000.

What is this for?

Supply-Justice

The custom in all our law courts is to have a picture of former justices and chief justices. In our Supreme court we have portraits of former chief justices, and this item is to provide for the portraits which we have not yet obtained. If my hon. friend will visit the Supreme court of Canada he will come to the conclusion that that building should be considerably improved. I think this very small item of $1,000 should be voted without any hesitation. The Supreme court is not what it should be.
The court or the building?

The building. I have no
criticism of the court, but I think it ought to be better lodged.
How many dozen do you get for this thousand dollars?
It depends on the artist.

I do not think there are portraits of the last two chief justices, Chief Justice Taschereau and Chief Justice Davies. There are portraits of Chief Justice Richards, Chief Justice Strong and Chief Justice Ritchie.
I think the intention is to complete the series.
Would not photographs be cheaper and twice as good?

Item agreed to.
Penitentiaries-Kingston-to provide pension at the rate of $600 per annum to Mrs. Violet
L.	Jenkin, widow of late penitentiary guard,
M.	E. Jenkin, from September 1, 1926 to March 31, 1927, $350.
On what basis is this pension granted?
On the basis of $50 a month up to March 31 of the present year. Then she will be drawing a pension as provided for in the main estimates.
Is this pension on the basis of the mother's allowance in certain provinces?
The 'basis is the precedent established in the department, that is, it is the amount that would be granted if there had been an award by the compensation board.

I think the pension is not sufficient. A widow with five children cannot possibly carry on on such a pension. The man was killed while on duty, and I 32649-1511
think the department should increase the amount. Under the mother's allowance legislation a widow with three children gets $54 a month.
At the rate of assessment under the Pension Act she would get a great deal more.

But that act does not cover these cases. I appreciate what my hon. friend says, and I will take the matter up with the officials. If there is any possibility of increasing the pension I am sure the department will do something further.
How long has this scale been in effect? I am informed it was established fifty years ago and has never been varied since.
The first payments in cases of this kind were made in 1913, and the same basis has prevailed ever since.
Of course the value of the dollar has gone down in the meantime.

There is another man in Kingston now, a complete invalid, who is receiving $25 or $26 a month. Whether he was injured while on duty through his own fault or not, it looks to me a pretty small piece of business. The guards are dealing with the most dangerous type of criminals, and one can appreciate the hazardous character of their duties by visiting the machine shop. This widow's husband was a bright young guard, and the minister must be aware that $600 a year is not sufficient to maintain her and her five children. The department ought to realize that the rate is too antiquated to meet present day conditions.

I believe it would meet the general approval of the committee if some arrangement could be made to increase this and similar votes. If this woman had been the widow of a judge I have no doubt she would be getting a much larger pension. A penitentiary guard has a much more dangerous job than a judge, and I think this amount should be increased.
The widows of judges do not get pensions.
They do not need any.
This is not by statute.

The law governs us in fixing the amount, but the money has to be voted by parliament.
Supply-Justice
On what basis do we grant these pensisns? When the Department of Mines estimates were up we granted some lady, supposed to be a widow, S3,000.
I understand from my colleague of the Interior that the item my hon. friend is referring to is a lump sum. This is a pension at the rate of $50 a month.

Mr. Chairman, is it not time that the government followed the example of the railways in providing for the dependents of officials killed while on duty? I cannot move an amendment to increase this vote, but surely the government will recognize that the stand I am taking is right.
I understand these cases are dealt with directly by the department, but the amounts paid are the same as would be paid by the compensation board.
If this widow could come under the Mother's Allowance Act of Ontario she would get more than the department is paying her. I think you should put the pension on the same basis as under that act.
I understand that that is the basis.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The duty of the government in considering oases of this kind is to treat them on a parity with the provisions of the compensation board of the particular province concerned. In the event jf accident or death the widow receives the pension she would have got had her husband been employed in similar service in the province. It is eminently fair.
I take it that I have the promise of the Solicitor General to go into the whole matter?
I surely will.

Item agreed to.
Amount required to pay amounts awarded to the United States government by the Pecuniary Claims Convention in the following cases:
The "Tattler" claim, $630.
The "G-erring Jr." claim, $9,000.

The Pecuniary Claims
Convention having concluded its labours, it is necessary for the various countries to arrange for the payment of awards made by the tribunal. The schedule considered by the tribunal comprises forty-one claims by the United States aggregating $5,515,958.29, and fifty-nine claims by the British government, including the claims of Canada and Newfoundland aggregating $5,717,138.75. Of these
fMr. Cannon.]
various claims thirty^two were awarded the United rStates totalling $81,113.06, and nineteen to the British government totalling $239,506.20. The United States government has appropriated funds to meet its indebtedness while the British and Newfoundland governments have undertaken to make similar provision. It is now the duty of Canada to take steps to pay the awards included in the above-mentioned cases. As the United States were awarded $81,000 and the British government, including Canada and Newfoundland, $239,000, it will be seen that we have made a fairly good bargain.

Item agreed to.
Litigated matters-To authorize payment of a special fee to C. P. Plaxton, K.C. for services in connection with the Labrador-Newfoundland case, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $2,500.
What is this $2,500 for?

Mr. Plaxton, of the Justice department, was entrusted with the preparation of the Labrador case and he did a good deal of extra work, having devoted his time to the task for several years. This amount is supplementary to his salary to compensate him for that extra work.
It is apart from his salary?
Yes.
Does he refund anything to the department for any time which he takes off?
I do not think he has lost any time.
If he takes a vacation does he refund anything?
I want to assure my hon. friend that the Labrador case is an important one and Mr. Plaxton has done very good work.

I do not wish to minimize the work of gentlemen of the legal profession but I must observe that their fees are becoming enormous. When we recall some of the events of the past twelve months I think it will be admitted that the legal profession is running crazy.
What about the government?

The government too. We are paying too much in fees and it is time w#

Supply-Justice
called a halt. Why should we pay a gratuity like this to a man who is in receipt of a permanent salary from the Department of Justice?
What about Rowell?
I have Rowell in mind.

What is the full
amount paid counsel in the Labrador case and what was the full amount paid the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty?

I am not in a position to state the exact amount that will be paid counsel in this case. As to the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty, the amount he received, as fixed in 1921, was $10,000. That covered work done during a period of five years and is certainly not exorbitant.
Carried.
It may be carried, but I protest.	.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police
Pay of force (including salaries of two constables, Ellesmere island district, at $2.25 per diem, to insure department against loss through death), $1,065,653.75.
Maintenance (including billeting, travelling expenses, forage, fuel and light, clothing, repairs and renewals, horses ammunition, stationery, etc., medical, hospital, etc., transportation and freight, buildings, repairs, contingencies and criminal investigations, and establishment of new detachments and renewals, $1,112,345.09.
To compensate members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for injuries received whilst in the performance of duty, $8,500.
To assist in enforcement of federal statutes (expenditure chargeable to this vote shall be in connection with such federal police duties as may be defined by the governor in council upon recommendation of the Minister of Justice, $75,000.
To provide for special services in connection with the enforcement of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, $25,000.

What is the reason
for the increase?

Forty-three new men
have been engaged in the northern sections of Canada.
What part" of the northern section, west or east?
Some of them will be employed in Baffin island-and others in Hudson bay and on the Mackenzie river, in the northernmost sections of the country.

Are any of the police to
be used in the Peace river district for the protection of ballot boxes?
I hope so. We shall have a few years to prepare for that emergency.

Has anything
been done to reinstate those police who were removed a few days prior to the last election? In Saskatchewan, I believe, two or three officers of the mounted police were removed, one from Prince Rupert and another from the Yukon territory, because they were Liberals. The idea was that they should not be able to use their influence nor to vote. At the same t'ime I believe one man was appointed aide de camp to the lieutenant governor in Regina, and that man is the president of the Conservative organization of that city.

I am glad to hear the
observations made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, who knows so much about everything, because what he has said indicates that these men should be very thankful they were not dismissed from the service. He says they were prevented from using their influence, being Liberals; apparently they desired to take part in the elections and1 that would1 have brought about their dismissal, in accordance with the observations made last night by the Postmaster General (Mr. Yeniot). As it is they should be thankful they were moved and not removed entirely from the public service for using their influence on behalf of the Liberal party in the election. The truth is that the gentlemen were moved on the strength of reports made by the superintendent, who sits on the floor of this House at the moment. With my own eyes I saw the report, which was received some months previously, and which suggested1 that they should be removed not because of their political faith but in the interests of the force. That report is a matter of record in the Department of Justice and can easily be brought down to substantiate my statement; it was on the strength of that report that these men were removed.
If the hon. gentleman desires to investigate the movement of men at the public expense from Toronto to Regina, on vouchers which can now be found in the department, in order that they might vote at Regina in the election of 1925, he would not have a great deal of difficulty in so doing. I would like to inform him that in that case the vouchers under which they were removed disclosed the fact that they were sent to Regina to vote at the public expense. These vouchers were subsequently altered, because
Supply-Justice

that was thought to be even too raw to go through the department files. That is the position if the hon. gentleman desires to know it.

I will state in reply that
I will make inquiries into the facts brought to my attention to-night, and the House may rest assured that the efficiency of the service will not suffer by any action which may be taken.
If the statement is true, would it not require some further evidence that this was done to prevent them from using their influence?

I would ask the Solicitor General if he would ask the commissioner of police as to the advisability of providing police posts in the different parts of Canada with automobiles. I have a case in mind in my own riding; it is a place called Emerson, where two mounted policemen are stationed. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because it was directed to me by the citizens of the district. These men do a lot of work for the revenue department, going around hunting up private stills and so forth, and I think their work would be much more efficient if they were provided with a small automobile in order to carry out their operations.
Automobiles will be supplied1 gradually as the needs arise.

Are any of the mounted
police now being used' in the suppression Of smuggling, and if so, where? While I am on my feet I would like to call the attention Of the Solicitor General to the necessity of sending a force in the coming spring, if the preventive service is not manned by that time, into the county of Kent, New Brunswick, where smuggling in alcoholic liquors is rampant.

A certain number of officers of the force were put under the Customs department last summer, and are still with that department but in a decreasing number. My hon. friend will recall that a considerable sum was voted last night for the organization of the preventive service, and we hope that the Customs department will take hold of the entire preventive service in order that the mounted police will be freer to perform the duties allotted to this force, and those duties only.
I would ask the Solicitor General if the government is considering adjourning very soon; it is now two o'clock.

I may say to my hon.
friend that a very good way to expedite adjournment would be to help me through my estimates.
I do not know about that. Some of us have been around the building since nine o'clock this morning and we are tired.

I just wanted to reiterate the position I have taken in recent years; it seems to me that there is unnecessary duplication as between the federal authorities and the provinces. I am not sure why it is necessary for us to have so many of the federal police stationed within the organized territories. I noticed a year or so ago a speech by Mr. Brownlee, the premier of Alberta, in which he protested against the mounted police in that district. I would ask why the Dominion government, in the face of a protest of that kind, still persist in maintaining the mounted police in the organized provinces.

The question of how the administration of justice and the police work in the provinces should be handled is now under study. I have had occasion to discuss the matter with the provincial authorities, and I can assure my hon. friend that we will try to devise the best possible methods as between the federal and provincial authorities, in order that both may remain within the scope of their jurisdiction.
Does the Solicitor General recognize the fact that there has been a great deal of duplication?
There has been.
