Item agreed to.
To assist in the suppression of the white slave traffic, $2,500.
What can be done with $2,500?

This is to cover expenses incurred in occasional cases where the mounted police have to deal with white slavery. The amount is not very large because this is only in exceptional cases. The cases are usually dealt with by the police authorities in the different cities.
How much was spent last year?
A few hundred' dollars.

Item agreed to.
Pensions-to provide for an annual pension from April 1, 1926, based on a widow's pension, under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police statutes, to Mrs. Letitia Kennedy, widow of the late Inspector G. W. Kennedy, deceased July 14, 1922. prior to the enactment of chapter 66, 1924, $423.50.

With respect to this item and the following one for a pension to Mrs. Caroline Elizabeth Mcll'lree, I am in great difficulty. The effect of these items is to give the widows a privileged position on the assumption that had their husbands lived to a certain date, they would have received a larger pension. I recently had occasion to bring to the attention of the department the fact that men who took their superannuation allowances in the force while the bonus was being paid which was subsequently made a part of their salary, received a much smaller pension than they would have received had they waited a few months longer and received the benefit of the increased salary. These pensions are based on the assumption that the increased salary had been paid. This widow is being paid on the basis of the 1924 pension and this is making it retroactive, while men who remained in the force, who took their pension and who are still living, have been refused the benefits of the amending legislation that a short time after increased the salaries of their successors by making the cost of living bonus a part of the salary.
I am informed that this is to meet the inconvenience suffered by this lady owing to the fact that by a technicality she did not have a pension at the time of-
The change in the legislation.
Yes. But the point made by my hon. friend is that we are increasing the pension so as to make it as high as it would have been if her husband had lived longer.
Yes.
That is not the case. It is to recoup her for what money she did not receive through some technicality.
Is this a permanent addition to her pension?
Yes.
We have just voted one pension to this lady and we are now voting another.
No, that is to cover the 1927 pension.
But this is an additional pension. She will be receiving two pensions.

I am sure that if she is
getting two pensions, somebody will soon find it out and it will be reduced to one.

Will the minister look
at the next item and see what it says:
To provide for an increase, from May 18, 1925, in the annual pension of $962.50 granted under section 51, chapter 91, revised statutes of 1906-as amended-to Mrs. Caroline Elizabeth Mclllree, widow of the late ex-Assistant Commissioner J. II. Mclllree, Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who died on May 17, 1925, said pension to be increased to $1,303.75 per annum, the amount to which she would have been entitled had she been eligible therefor under the increase in police pensions granted by chapter 24, 15-16 George V, an act to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act.
That is exactly as I put the matter to my hon. friend. I recently had occasion to take up with the department the case of a superintendent who retired just before this amendment was put through and who is now receiving the smaller pension that this widow was receiving, and who, had he received the benefits she is receiving, would have got a few hundred dollars more of a pension. As he served his full period he receives a total pension which is equivalent to seven-tenths of hii salary. If he had waited until the statute referred to was enacted ; he would! have received that increase. He did not receive it, and now we are'giving it to the widow although we declined it to the living man.
Supply-Justice

These items are t'o meet
changes introduced in 1924, but not to cover the bonus to which my hon. friend is alluding.
No, the increased salary.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police-maintenance including $100 to reimburse ex-eonstable E. H. Woolams, loss of personal effects in the Northwest Territories and revote of $76,197.25 for special northern services in the western Arctic subdistrict, $76,297.25.

A few years ago
quite a number of members on this side of the House raised their voices against the large amounts being spent in this country on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and I recall plainly that Sir Lomer Gouin, then Minister of Justice, decreased the estimates for the mounted police. We have just passed one vote providing for an increase of $237,000, which in my estimation is a very large vote. Of course, I appreciate that it is difficult for a private member to understand whether or not some of these estimates are justified, but as we have already voted one large increase I think we should have some explanation of this item.

The increase is easily
understood. The work of the force has been extended, and therefore the personnel has been increased. As to whether the force should be increased or not, that is a matter of policy which might be discussed, but with the increase in the duties of the force this extra amount is required.
Is this $76,000 to provide for an increase in the force?

There is no increase in
the force this year. This is a revote.
If there has been no increase in the force why should we vote $237,000 more than last year?

As I stated before in
answer to one of my hon. friends, we are establishing new (stations in the northern section of the country.

Item agreed to.
Public archives, $90,000.

We have just passed
one item for public archives. Why are there two different items?

This is a cumulative
amount covering branches of the Archives department throughout the Dominion, in Montreal and the maritime provinces, also

branches of the Archives department in London and Paris. The rest of the amount is required to make purchases of manuscripts, pictures and historical documents which we keep in the Archives building at Ottawa.
What is the salary now paid to the Dominion Archivist?

That is all he
receives?
As archivist.

Expenses in connection with the Early French Colonial Historical Exhibition in Paris, $2,500.

This is a revote for an
exhibition that is to take place in Paris next year of early French colonial establishments.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend
from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has just left the chamber. He is very much interested in this bill, and has an important amendment to move to it. I do not wish
to press the measure, but it is important that it should pass so that it may go to the Senate. It is an important piece of legislation. It was understood that it would be given third reading to-night, but if the hon. leader of the opposition desires to have it stand over until to-morrow, we should take it up first thing in the morning.

I would like it the very
